speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a question of privilege, a good question of privilege. So that I will be fully understood by the Minister of Finance I will try to state my question of privilege in English, and in doing so I should like to ask for the clemency of members of the house.
My question of privilege arises out of the estimates for the year 1964-65 and the statement made in the house by the Minister of Finance. I quote from page 451 of Hansard of Tuesday, March 3, 1964, the English edition:
For example, the public debt charges, which are statutory, are shown in 1964-65 at some $157 million more than the amount included in the main estimates for 1963-64 In fact, Mr. Speaker, the increase anticipated in 1964-65 over the expected actual expenditure in 1963-64 is about $52 million. This indicates a serious underestimate in the amount presented to parliament in the 1963-64 estimates.
If hon. members will take a sheet of paper and a pencil they will understand the figures I am about to point out. In 1963-64 the estimate for public debt charges was $881 million. In 1964-65 the same charges are $1,037 million. The Minister of Finance says that the real increase is $52 million. The difference between $1,037 million and $881 million leaves about $156 million. Less the real increase of $52 million, that means that the underestimate for the previous year is about $104 million. If we add the increase of $104 million to the previous estimates for 1963-64 of $881 million, that means that the charges on the public debt in 1963-64 actually cost us $985 million. If we subtract the same amount of $104 million from the present figure in the 1964-65 estimates of $1,037 million that means that the cost of the debt in 1964-65 will be $933 million. This means, Mr. Speaker, not an increase but a decrease of $52 million in the actual amount of interest on the public debt.
This is impossible, Mr. Speaker; first, because there has been no reimbursement of the debt; second, because there has been a deficit of many hundreds of millions of dollars; third, because the minister said in his statement there was an increase of $52 million. This means that the actual figures for the cost in 1964-65 will be, first, the amount estimated in 1963-64, $881 million, plus the underestimation for this year of $104 million, plus the surplus in the estimates for 1964-65 amounting to $52 million. These figures total the exact cost of the debt charges in 1964-65, namely $1,037 million.
I believe that the procedure employed by the Minister of Finance was completely irregular and wrong. The Minister of Finance presented his estimates for 1964-65 on March 3. On March 6, he presented supplementary estimates-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSING OF FOUR RADAR STATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSING OF FOUR RADAR STATIONS
speechtext:
Last week a number of hon. gentlemen, including the hon. member for Ville-neuve and the hon. member for Simcoe East, asked about radar stations. I should now like to make a short statement in this connection.
A review has been made of the early radar warning lines in order to ascertain whether economies could be made without reducing the over-all effectiveness of the system. As a result of this review, and following consultation with United States and NORAD authorities, it has been decided to close down four radar stations of the R.C.A.F.'s Pine Tree radar line; R.C.A.F. stations Edgar, Ontario; St. Sylvestre and Parent, Quebec, and Beaverbank, Nova Scotia.
Pine Tree radar stations were established as a joint venture with the United States, and negotiations have now been completed to coordinate the details of the deactivation.
Some units of the Pine Tree line in eastern Canada, which were among the first to be completed, became operational in 1952. Radar equipment was not as powerful or reliable as it is today, and the stations were constructed relatively close together. However, the detection and tracking capabilities of radar stations have improved, through automation and other means, to the extent that it is now possible to reduce the density of radar sites in eastern Canada.
Approximately 700 military and 300 civilian manpower positions will be affected by the closing of the four radar bases. It is intended to reassign service personnel to help alleviate

National Defence
current shortages in other R.C.A.F. high priority programs. Additionally, the Department of National Defence will collaborate with other departments of the government in an attempt to alleviate any hardship that might be caused to civilian employees of these radar stations.
It is intended to close down the bases as rapidly as possible, and closure is expected to be generally completed this summer. An annual saving of some $6 million in operating and maintenance costs currently associated with the four stations will be realized.
A number of air defence radar stations in the United States were closed out last year, as were doppler stations in Canada forming part of the D.E.W. line. Earlier this year the deactivation of part of the mid-Canada line, built and maintained by Canada, was announced.

WELFARE SERVICES TO INDIANS
speechtext:
1.	Does the federal government have any agreements with the provinces under which welfare departments of provincial governments provide welfare services for Indians on reserves and, if so, to what extent are such services provided?
2.	Does the federal government have an agreement with the provincial government of British

Columbia relating to social welfare services among the Indians in the Fort Nelson area, and, if so, what are the terms of such agreement?

subtopic: WELFARE SERVICES TO INDIANS
speechtext:
1. Yes.
(a)	An agreement between the federal government and the province of Manitoba provides for the extension of child welfare services to the reserves within the area of jurisdiction of the children's aid society of western Manitoba, (b) Child welfare services are available to all reserves in Ontario through an over-all agreement between the federal government and the provincial government and the children's aid societies, (c) An agreement between the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government allows for the extension of child welfare services to all reserves in Nova Scotia, (d) The federal and Yukon Territorial governments have an agreement whereby the territorial government assumes responsibility for the administration of child welfare services and the federal government makes an annual financial contribution toward the administrative costs.
2. Yes, by agreement between the federal government and the government of the province of British Columbia, the province provides welfare assistance to Indians who are living off reserves. The costs of assistance to Indians who have lived less than a year on a self supporting basis in a non-Indian community are refunded by the federal government. It is also provincial policy to extend child welfare services to Indians and non-Indians, though there is no formal agreement on this with the province. Both the agreement on welfare assistance and the informal arrangements on child welfare services apply in the Fort Nelson area. In practice, however, these services are affected by the availability of provincial staff and the thoroughness with which they can cover a large geographic area.
Under the national welfare grants program of the Department of National Health and Welfare the British Columbia department of social welfare submitted a project in 1963-64 to extend child welfare services administered by its district office at Fort St. John. This particular office also serves the Alaska highway on which Fort Nelson is situated. It provides services for the entire population including Indians, in Fort Nelson and the surrounding area.
Expenditures under this project have been approved up to $13,002.50 in 1963-64 with similar expenditures to be made in future years. These expenditures will be shared equally by the federal and provincial governments. Under this project the provincial government expects to survey the area in terms of staff needs to meet the variety of

social problems in the community, the development of resources to meet children's needs, and planning for foster children which involves both the adoption and home finding programs of the provincial welfare department.

PUBLIC WORKS INSPECTION OF EMBASSIES ABROAD
speechtext:
1.	Does the Department of Public Works make periodic inspections of the buildings and grounds of Canadian embassies abroad and, if so, on what
basis?
2.	What inspections have been made in the last five years of embassy facilities in Paris, Bonn, Copenhagen, Rome and Brussels, and by whom?
3.	As a result of such inspections, what effective maintenance was carried out and by whom?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS INSPECTION OF EMBASSIES ABROAD
speechtext:
1. With the exception of the offices of the Canadian high commissioner in Canada House in London, England, the Department of Public Works does not carry out periodic inspections of the buildings and grounds of Canadian embassies abroad. This is normally done by members of the staff of the supplies and properties division of the Department of External Affairs. From time to time when the pressure of work has precluded such inspections being carried out by external affairs, and when specific or urgent problems have arisen, this department has not hesitated to call upon the Department of Public Works for assistance. For example the chief architect of the Department of Public Works inspected a number of missions in the Far East in the summer of 1963 at the request of external affairs.
2.	(a) Paris. The government owned offices and the government owned official residence are inspected frequently by Mr. A. Monette, external affairs departmental architect, who has his office in the Canadian embassy in that city.
(b)	Bonn. The office, a rented property, was inspected by Mr. J. A. Zoubie, a technical officer in the Department of External Affairs. The official residence, a rented property, was inspected by Mr. W. C. Jaquith, a technical officer in the Department of External Affairs.
(c)	Copenhagen. The offices (rented property) and the government owned official residence were inspected by Mr. A. Monette, external affairs departmental architect.
(d)	Rome. The government owned offices were inspected by Mr. A. Monette, external affairs departmental architect. The official residence, a rented property, was inspected by Mr. W. C. Jaquith, a technical officer in the Department of External Affairs.
(e)	Brussels. The government owned offices and the government owned official residence are inspected at regular intervals by Mr. A. Monette, external affairs departmental architect.

Questions
3.	(a) Paris. Contracts for cleaning, the maintenance of the grounds, heating systems and elevators of the offices and the official residence are let each year after tenders have been called by the embassy. Acoustic tile has been installed in various reception or meeting areas, windows have been weather stripped and a phased program of redecoration is being carried out in the office building. The official residence has been completely redecorated by the lowest of three tenderers.
(b)	Bonn. *A phased program of redecoration is being carried out in the office building, floors have been repaired and linoleum replaced where necessary. The heating system has been converted to oil with the cost being borne equally by the owner and the embassy. The official residence has been redecorated.
(c)	Copenhagen. *Minor repairs only have been necessary in these offices which are located in a building which is only four years old.
The exterior of the official residence has been repointed and redecorated, the plumbing and electrical systems and the roof have been repaired after tenders were called.
(d)	Rome. The walls and floors of the offices were strengthened to carry the weight of safes, file cabinets etc., water tanks were replaced, doors and tile floors were repaired, a new switchboard was installed, minor repairs were carried out on the heating system, the plumbing system and the roof and part of the interior was redecorated-all under contract. *Only minor repairs were carried out at the official residence.
(e)	Brussels. The exterior of the office building was repointed, the windows repaired and redecorated. The third floor and part of the basement was repartitioned and redecorated. The wiring of the building was replaced and the floors and flooring repaired or replaced, all under contract. The residence is a new building completed in 1963 and maintenance costs are therefore at a minimum. A contract has been let for maintenance of the grounds.
*This denotes leased properties. Considerable difficulty is experienced in persuading owners to maintain them in a manner
acceptable to the department. Only after all means of persuasion are exhausted does the department undertake to carry maintenance on these properties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want at this time to move a motion, and I understand that this is the appropriate place to do it. I might say that a similar motion is being moved at this time in the Ontario legislature by my provincial colleague, Stephen Lewis.
I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster, the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the critical shortage of hospital beds and hospital accommodation in metropolitan Toronto.
This is a matter of national significance, Mr. Speaker, and I would appreciate being heard on the question of urgency. You were good enough to indicate that one of the tests for a motion of this type is that it be of national significance. I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this serious and critical situation in metropolitan Toronto is a matter that affects every member of the house.
The reason I say this is that because of the degree of specialization in the metro hospitals, patients are treated from every part of Canada and from every part of North America. Therefore any critical shortage in staff or facilities of the Toronto hospitals vitally affects the constituencies of members of this house and the people in them.
Hospital Bed Shortage
As far as urgency is concerned, about which I suggest there can be absolutely no question, at the present time doctors and hospitals in the municipality of metropolitan Toronto are being forced to turn away people who urgently need treatment. People with cancer or any other disease of that type have to wait as much as six months for a bed. Not very long ago because a young child could not get into one hospital, the child died in the middle of Bloor street viaduct while in transit to another hospital. At any given time there are over 7,000 people waiting for operations of one kind or another. So the matter of urgency and criticalness of debate seems to be without question.
The other test is whether an opportunity will be available to debate this question at some other time. I suggest there is no such other opportunity. The throne speech debate is no longer before us; the government has forecast a series of legislative measures which will keep us tied up for the next two or three weeks, so there does not seem to me to be an opportunity to debate this topic. We have tried to raise the matter on orders of the day. We have tried to raise it on the order paper. Delegations have visited the minister. I am sure representations have come from Toronto members on the government side, either privately or in caucus, but we are still getting the same old brush-off.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter of critical national importance. It affects not only the community from which I come but the people in all constituencies right across the country.

Generally speaking the rules are, of course, that the subject should be national in scope and of urgent necessity for consideration, and that the opportunity for debate is not just around the corner. In the present case I ask the question, is the matter of a shortage of hospital beds and hospital accommodation generally speaking a federal matter?
Adjournment under standing order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the federal government. Looking at the request quickly, from a procedural point of view I would say that what is contemplated by standing order 26 is an occurrence of a very sudden emergency. If hon. members refer to citation 100 (8) of Beauchesne they will see that this general matter has been discussed many, many years ago. May I also add that the adjournment of the house cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the government of Canada yet given an answer to the secretary general of the United Nations regarding the provision of a force for Cyprus? If so, what is the answer? If there has been no determination made yet, is the reason for the delay the prohibitive cost that would have to be borne by the various nations making contributions? Is the fact that the United Nations itself is not going to pay for any portion of the peace keeping machinery, and that the rule has been established that each nation making a contribution to the force will have to pay the cost itself, not something that will weaken the United Nations in its peace keeping operations and, indeed, will place the United Nations in the position of being subject to the veto of every nation which refuses to contribute?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to this question I would say that the arrangements for the necessary financing of the peace keeping operation are not in the present circumstances an obstacle to action on our part. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that this peace keeping operation would be more truly in keeping with the United Nations if the financing of the operation were borne by the United Nations itself. However, the financial situation of the United Nations is such that the financing of this peace keeping operation is not possible, just as it was not possible in the case of the establishment of the observation mission in the Yemen.
The situation with regard to the proposed establishment of an international force continues to be the subject of intensive consultations among Canada, the secretary general and the proposed participants. The fact that the emergency in Cyprus primarily involves two communities, makes it essential that any outside forces which may be committed as part of the United Nations peace keeping force should have a very clear idea of their powers and responsibilities, as well as a full assurance of the co-operation of the two communities.

It is for this reason that each country which has been approached for a force contribution has sought clarification of a number of fundamental points concerning the role of the force in these difficult circumstances. These points are being discussed at this very moment at the United Nations.

The resolution of the security council is in very general terms, and the powers given to the secretary general are likewise in very general terms. These are now being discussed with the proposed participants. One of the countries invited has definitely refused to participate. Two of the other countries, that does not include Canada, have laid down important financial considerations. The terms of reference of the force have not yet been established, and there are other factors requiring clarification to make the force an effective body in preserving the peace in an area where peace is now being preserved by 7,000 British troops, the total number that would be encompassed by the proposed international force.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE

maintopic: CONSTRUCTION OF ROAD FROM YUKON TO ARCTIC COAST

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CONSTRUCTION OF ROAD FROM YUKON TO ARCTIC COAST
speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. On Wednesday last I asked the hon. gentleman if he would make a full statement to the house with respect to the government's development road policy, particularly with regard to the 400 mile road to be constructed in the Yukon through to the Arctic coast. At that time the hon. gentleman said he would take the question as notice, and I am wondering if he is now in a position to give an answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: CONSTRUCTION OF ROAD FROM YUKON TO ARCTIC COAST
speechtext:
I am certain the hon. gentleman will agree that transportation in the general area he has in mind is a multi-pronged affair involving better facilities for transportation by water on the Mackenzie and improved transportation by air, through the development of landing fields, as well as by road. I am sure, too, the hon. member is aware that the present road goes to a point just below the Arctic circle; to Chapman lake, I think. Surveys have been made in the area in accordance with the policy established by the previous government, which we hope
Inquiries of the Ministry we can realize, with a view to getting a road substantially to the Arctic by 1970, which was the target date.
Three different suggestions have been made. The first is the extension of the present road beyond Chapman. Another is that the route should follow the Mackenzie river. The third is that it should run in the direction of McKay lake. I am sure the hon. member for Yukon, and particularly the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, will appreciate that the prospect of a highway right through to the Arctic is an ambition likely to fall short of realization in the face of the difficulties presented by the fantastic delta of the Mackenzie river. Nevertheless, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the government is working in this direction, and we hope to develop properties, mineral claims and oil discoveries, as we go along. This too will help determine the particular direction in which a move will be made.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: POSSIBLE AMENDMENT RESPECTING FIREARMS FOR SPORTING PURPOSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Can he say whether consideration is being given to amending legislation covering the control of sporting firearms and ammunition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: POSSIBLE AMENDMENT RESPECTING FIREARMS FOR SPORTING PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, neither my department nor, so far as I am aware, any other department has given any consideration to imposing limitations which will restrict the right of any citizen in a lawful manner to own or use firearms for such purposes as hunting and recreation, subject to two minor exceptions.
These are that in connection with a study now being made of the firearms sections in my department, consideration is being given, in the ordinary way, to suggestions that the age limits relating to the possession of firearms by juveniles be raised, and that a registrar should, in certain cases, be authorized to refuse registration of a pistol or a revolver, thus making continued possession illegal on the part of the applicant. subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, March 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East):
That the treaty between Canada and the United States of America relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, signed at Washington on January 17, 1961, together with the protocol containing modifications and clarifications to the treaty annexed to an exchange of notes between the governments of Canada and the United States signed on January 22, 1964, be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
There remains but little to be dealt with after the debate which has gone on, as it has, for several days. I would point out that, though we are engaged in a debate on a resolution that the treaty under consideration be referred to the standing committee on external affairs, the committee in question has, as yet, not been set up or constituted in any way.
I am sure the house listened with great interest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin, Essex East) as he reviewed the situation connected with this treaty-how, at his very best, in mellifluous words, he paid tribute to the Conservative party as the government of the day which brought this treaty about. Indeed, if I may say so, Orpheus, with all his legendary powers, with all his ability to charm the birds off the trees by the sweetness of his remarks, would surely have paid a tribute in that connection to the Secretary of State for External Affairs had he been able to look down from above.
He gave us a great deal of credit. The treaty which we executed received the imprimatur of his approval. Indeed it was difficult to understand why there had been the criticism of past days, after the eulogy that was delivered on the former government and its actions in this connection. Following his course, I intend to refer to the signing of the treaty and also to some statements made at that time by the representatives for Canada, which should be on the record.
As was said over and over again, the treaty was signed on January 17, 1961. At that time I said it represented a major advance in co-operation by the two nations without the sacrifice of the rights, the sovereignty or otherwise of either country, and was indeed a landmark in responsible joint action by nations for their economic betterment. I would point out immediately that when we signed

Columbia River Treaty the treaty there had never been any indication that Premier Bennett of British Columbia was not in agreement with its terms. It was only after signature had been given to the treaty that he, for the first time, raised certain objections in that connection. I recall that on September 16, 1961, some months thereafter, he said-and I quote-that Ottawa was ready to sacrifice British Columbia. From the beginning he wanted the downstream power sold in the United States. He wanted that for his own purposes, although at no time while the negotiations were going on was there any question whatsoever of the unacceptability of that treaty to the province of British Columbia.
You have heard, sir, from various hon. members from British Columbia. You have heard from the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming), the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton), and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Willoughby). Each and all have set out, not only their own views but also those of the people they represent. It comes as a great surprise to me that the members of the government should today be so eulogistic of the treaty which only a few short months ago represented, they said, a loss of Canadian sovereignty. I intend to refer to some of those statements and to point out the fact that either they were sincere during two election campaigns, and are not today; or they are today, and they were not then. They had spokesmen on this matter. There was the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Davis). He is an expert-

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: On what?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
-on the question of power; an outstanding young man. But it is hard to understand how one so expert could have been so wrong in 1961 when he entered the field of journalism through articles written in the Vancouver Sun. I intend to refer at some length to his remarks in that connection, because the other day as I listened to him I could only conclude that, with all his expertness, he found almost insurmountable difficulty in explaining the unexplainable position which he now takes as compared with the stand he took in 1961. A moment ago I said that at the time the treaty was signed a statement was made at the signing ceremony in Washington. In that statement I said this:
This is the first time that anywhere in the world an arrangement has been made between governments by which the operation of large water storages in one country produces vast benefits in another which are shared by both countries. The program envisaged under the treaty is based on skilled engineering and resourceful collaboration. The negotiating teams, under Mr. Elmer Bennett for the United States and Hon. E. D. Fulton for

Canada, have secured agreement on difficult and complex problems in a comparatively short time. Their task was performed with patience and in a spirit of compromise but without sacrifice or impairment of the independence and sovereignty of their respective countries.
Now, sir, those were our views then. They are our views now. I find it difficult to understand, however, the change of attitude on the part of those who sit opposite. I was greatly impressed, as I always am, by the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has the power of analysis and the embroidery of beautiful words. He performed his task with his accustomed finesse. However, I was surprised at the degree of commendation that we in the opposition, the former government of the day, rather belatedly received at his hands on behalf of the government. Indeed, as I listened to his speech and read it afterwards I could only conclude that after the vilification of two election campaigns we now have the vindication of the government of today in the course which we followed.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
That has not been unusual since the present government came into office. The Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the rewards of public life. As one who is dean of the House of Commons, he spoke with authority. He pointed out that this treaty was one that would be looked back on in the years ahead with his approval and the approval of the government. No greater tribute has ever been paid to the former government than was contained in the words he used. Sir, I pointed out a moment ago that it was not always so. Changes have taken place. A few short months ago they referred to the treaty as a deception. They referred to us as though we had obtained it under false pretences. They indicated their view that it was not a legitimate treaty which protected Canada's rights. Never was illegitimacy so briskly legitimized by any subsequent government as has taken place here.
A year and a half ago this treaty baby was unwanted, and now those who sit opposite, having put certain little declarations in the protocol, now claim the unwanted foundling as of their own paternity, and welcome it with great rejoicing. They touched it up a little-and I am going to refer to the touching up operation, because that is all it was. Then they decided that they would allow for the sale of the downstream benefits in the United States, and I shall deal with that during the course of my remarks.
Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, when they said that General McNaughton was right; that General McNaughton's criticisms, which were made months after the treaty was executed,

were well based? Now what do they say of General McNaughton? I recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), when he was on this side, wanting to adjourn the house a year ago because General McNaughton had said that the treaty had sold Canada down the river. What do they say of him today? Someone has said that he is a nice old fellow who does not know what he is talking about. A year or a year and a half ago the Liberal opposition were undertaking to bring about a new treaty which would embody the McNaughton views. Sir, never has there been so great a transition in the thinking of a political party as that which has been revealed by those who today sit on the treasury benches. They all had different views a year or so ago, but that is not unusual. This is a cabinet of dissenting views. We have had an example here today, where one minister expressed himself in the house. Instead of it being the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), a man learned in the law, it was the minister of defence. He made a speech over the week end in which he decided on the amendment of the constitution. He said that something had to be done, that it had to be reshaped, revised and rewritten. He was not talking about raids on this occasion; this provided a welcome relief from his own department.
Then what about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Another minister, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis), made a speech in which he said that the C.B.C. should mend its ways and stop helping separatism. When the question is asked today whether he is speaking for the government, the answer is certainly one of uncertainty. Then the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) goes to Winnipeg and says:
Sauve: Ce n'est pas par une legislation que nous sauverons l'unite du pays.
Then he proceeded to give his views. What a conglomeration of uncertainty sits opposite, with ministers speaking everywhere in a cacophony of voices and ideas.
But this is not new. This is what happened in connection with the treaty which we entered into with the United States when the election campaigns were on. It was said that Canada's rights were not protected. It was said that we had lost the right to divert the water from the Kootenay. It was said that the precedent had been set and created for other waters beside those of the Columbia covered by the agreement. And so it went on.
I now intend to refer first to the protocol and then to the various criticisms which were made by hon. gentlemen opposite. I point out immediately that the Columbia treaty was part and parcel of a policy which the former government wanted for national development. This was one of the great objectives of the
Columbia River Treaty former administration. For years the Columbia had been a football. For years its development had been considered, but it was not until we took office and until 1961 that an agreement was secured. We wanted to bring about in this nation a national grid whereby our electric power would be made available to other parts of the country. To that end we convened a conference to start preparations in consultation with the provinces. Today wherever developments are taking place, including the Peace river power project, we will have available the necessary power for such a grid if and when all the provinces will agree, as they did at that meeting, with the exception of the province of Quebec. We want to see power developed in all parts of Canada. We want to export wherever there is a surplus of power which has been certified by the national energy board. Indeed, we made provision for export of excess power in 1962 and changed the policy that existed in our country for a period of more than 50 years. We want to see power development in every part of Canada. We want to see the great resources of the Yukon river developed as a project for our country. We want to see the Nelson river harnessed. Only on Friday last in the legislature of Manitoba there was tabled a report which set out the tremendous potentialities that are to be found there. These were all part and parcel of our plans and ideas.
One of the developments which has been spoken of as a potentially great one is that of the Hamilton falls project in the province of Quebec. Within the last week or so doubts have been cast as to whether power produced by hydro can meet the competition of power produced by atomic energy. I read in the Vancouver Sun, which I am sure the parliamentary secretary will regard as an appropriate newspaper from which to quote, for he has become one of its correspondents, that-
*-Eastern Canada's biggest hydroelectric project is now in jeopardy because of competition from nuclear power.
Then the article goes on to refer to the $1 billion Hamilton falls project which would supply vast quantities of Labrador's hydroelectric power to Newfoundland, Quebec and New York state. Then it says:
The American market is crucial to the scheme's success. And now Westinghouse says it can supply New York with nuclear power for six mills, two mills less than the estimated cost of power from Labrador.
Since the Westinghouse offer was received, New York power officials have delayed signing the Labrador agreement.
In other words, action to assure these developments should be proceeded with at the earliest possible date.

Columbia River Treaty
What were the changes in the treaty, Mr. Speaker? There were no changes in the treaty. Had there been any substantial change this would not be a protocol to the treaty which is now placed before us, but the treaty would have had to be given once more consideration by the United States senate.
I am going to refer to the changes, though they are of little importance, of little consequence. They do not alter the purport and the objective of the treaty. My friends of the N.D.P. say it would be impossible to take any of the waters of the Kootenay in the years ahead, should we on the Saskatchewan river or elsewhere require them. I do not so interpret the treaty. I do not so interpret the expression "consumptive uses", an expression which, had it not been interpreted in the press release that was issued by the Department of External Affairs, would have left no doubt that it included the use of power. However, an interpretation has been given to it by the government of Canada and that interpretation in the years ahead will certainly be used adversely against us.
They say that we sacrificed Canadian sovereignty. This is the first time, Mr. Speaker, that the government of which I had the honour to be the head was ever charged with bending to the demands of the United States government. We protected Canada's sovereignty. That was the essence of the arguments that were used against us, that we were anti-American when in fact we were proCanadian.
We want to preserve our Canadian waters. We started this in the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project in the province of Saskatchewan. We must take action in this connection. We must assure that the profligate use of Canada's waters, which 20 or 30 years ago appeared to be beyond waste, ceases, and that these waters are preserved for future generations. We are rich in many resources, but I believe our greatest asset is our water resource. As I said a moment ago, we have been profligate in its use. Conservation of water is a necessity for Canadian growth. Water tables are diminishing. We can already see the day when our water resources will have been reduced to a point where they will not meet Canadian needs of the future. The United States already sees itself as an importer of water from Canada. Last year a United States senator stated that the day was not far distant when it would be necessary to import water from Canada.
I interpolate at this point to say that Canadians today need to know about these resources. A dominion-provincial survey should be made of our waters to the end that, in co-operation with the provinces, we will arrive at plans that will assure that these

water resources shall be available for future generations. In the province of Saskatchewan action has been taken in this connection by a bill now before the legislature of Saskatchewan entitled "the water resources bill". However, we need more than that. We need action taken nationally, so that these waters will be preserved in their purity and so that waste shall be prevented under law. As part of our national plan of development we brought into effect legislation to encourage anti-pollution measures.
I said a moment ago that the Columbia was one of the plans we had in mind in respect of the development of this nation. What happened? As soon as we had the signatures of the United States and Canada affixed to the treaty Premier Bennett stepped in. He did not want to have 50 per cent of the downstream benefits brought back to Canada. We felt that they should be brought back, in that they would provide British Columbia with low cost power, or lower cost power than would otherwise have been the case. Now they are being sold. It is not for me to condemn the decision in that connection. The people of British Columbia had an election and they determined that was what they wanted done. They wanted the downstream benefits sold in the United States. That does not alter our view that a mistake has been made, but it also bears out that what is being done today under the protocol carries out not only the views of Premier Bennett and his government but also the views of the people of the province of British Columbia, as expressed in an election campaign.
What is this? A treaty? I say it is a series of explanatory notes. These are cascades of words indicating that changes have been made and improvements brought about whereas in general, with the exception of the downstream benefits, there is little or no change. Let me read the summary which appears on page 4 of the press release issued by the Department of External Affairs on January 22 last.
Among improvements through the protocol to the treaty are:
(a)	New procedures for Canadian participation in determining the need for any flood control requested by the United States...
(b)	Reaffirmation in positive terms of Canada's right to make any diversions of Columbia basin water required for consumptive needs such as irrigation and municipal uses.
You do not need interpretation of what is clear. This is simply stating that what was decided, was decided.
(c)	Clarification of Canada's right to continue in perpetuity any diversions of Kootenay river water-
That required no clarification, except that the Liberal party felt that there was something wrong here, and I will deal with that at some length.

(d)	Confirmation of Canadian control over the detailed operation of the Canadian treaty storage for power purposes.
What was confirmed? What was confirmed was what appeared in the treaty. It does not need confirmation, but for the purpose of pretending that vast changes had been made these words were inserted in the press release.
(e)	An increase in Canada's downstream energy benefits by 14 to 18 per cent by using a longer period of streamflow in benefit calculations.
(f)	A clear statement that the treaty does not establish any principle or precedent that applies to any waters other than those of the Columbia river basin-
Who said it did? It was those people sitting over there who said it. No confirmation or clarification was needed. The treaty said that it was made with reference to the Columbia. It did not say that this would be a precedent from now on, but they had to put that statement in there and in the protocol to give the pretence that they were making a change. Then the press release goes on to say:
The total effect of the improvements through the protocol is to establish a better balance between essentially Canadian interests and the interests of the Columbia river basin as a whole.
What does that mumbo-jumbo mean? It is simply words. They know that the treaty was not changed in any particular to such an extent as to require reconsideration by the United States senate.
Then, having criticized this treaty with all the abandon of the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Davis), joined in by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), they had to produce something. They produced the protocol, which is nothing more nor less than an explanation of that which required no explanation, plus the two changes to which I have made reference.
Let me read part of the protocol. Here is something classic, and it ends up this way:
Canada and the United States of America are in agreement that article XIII, subsection 1 of the treaty provides to each of them a right to divert water for a consumptive use.
Why wouldn't they be in agreement; that is what is provided?
Then, another part of the protocol reads as follows:
Any diversion of water from the Kootenay river when once instituted under the provisions of article XIII of the treaty is not subject to any limitation as to time.
It never was. However, this was uttered in such stentorian tones for the purpose of indicating the vast changes that have taken place. There are pages of stuff like that, and it finally ends up by saying this:
Columbia River Treaty
Canada and the United States of America are in agreement that the treaty does not establish any general principle or precedent applicable to waters, other than those of the Columbia basin-
Who said it did? These people sitting over there, in order to pretend that they were bringing about tremendous changes, had their interpretation of what the treaty said placed in the protocol. It has been a wonderful exercise in pretence. They had to do something like this. They said the treaty was wrong. They said we sold out Canada. They said we did not protect the interests of our nation. Well, having said that, there was nothing that they could do but produce the protocol to bolster up their pretence.
I intend now to refer in general to some of the things that were stated by those who today sit opposite. It has been very interesting. It is most revealing. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and those associated with him have taken a stand which, whether I agree with it or not, represents consistency. They took a stand, an understandable one from their point of view. But what of these people who sit opposite today and who wrap themselves in the garments of treaty-making perfection? What of them; what did they say? There has been a complete disregard in that protocol, and in the support they give the treaty today, of the pledged word of the Prime Minister. He said there would be renegotiation of the treaty. There has not been any renegotiation of the treaty. I will refer to the definition of renegotiation as it came from the lips of one who speaks with that authority that lies only with the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. It was he who led the Prime Minister along the garden path.
It was beneficial to take the stand that we had sold out Canada. This stand got them votes in British Columbia. Now they beat a retreat from the stand that they took, and in beating that retreat they put up a smoke screen in the form of a protocol. They say, see what great changes we have wrought in our name. This is just an example of the unctuous way in which they speak of this treaty, of the cynical manner in which they have broken their promises. They pretend now that changes were made. I know it is a dangerous thing to disagree with an expert, but when the expert enters the field of writing and writes down in detail his views, then has to swallow them afterwards, this certainly become a difficult task in political digestion. This is what his position is. Let me read from what he wrote. I ask the house to realize that I do not want to read excerpts from the statement because this would not give a true picture. However, I do not want to clutter the record with all that he said. If

Columbia River Treaty at any time the hon. member wants to rise and suggest to me that I have left out anything that is beneficial to him, I shall certainly include it.
I should like to refer to an article entitled "Present Columbia River Treaty Ties Canada's Hands", written by the Liberal member of parliament for Coast-Capilano. There is a reference to his qualifications, and they are great. He headed the Liberal party's committee on power and energy during the last parliament, and he also headed the Prime Minister along the road that caused him to say the treaty into which we had entered was detrimental to Canada. Let us read a few excerpts from this article as an indication of the author's attitude. There are five principal points, and this is No. 1:
The present Columbia river treaty is not good enough. It amounts to a sell-out of our Canadian resources.
If it did, does the protocol not do the same when it approves of the treaty? Then, the article goes on:
This embarrassing treaty must therefore be renegotiated-renegotiated in such a way as to make low cost power available to us as consumers in British Columbia.
In what way does the low cost power become available through renegotiation? What does he mean by "renegotiation"? I will define what he means by "renegotiation". The hon. member refers to the framework of a new treaty, and a little later in the article says that a new treaty, phrased in terms of principle should come first. Apparently what was meant by "renegotiation", was a new treaty. This is what he said.
Let me read some of the statements in this article:
We must act quickly to make a new agreement with the Americans on the Columbia, an agreement which would be more flexible, which would permit an early start on agreed projects and a delay of the more controversial ones.
Is there anything in the protocol that delays the more controversial ones? Is there anything in the protocol that bears out those words concerning what was going to take place? I have looked. He said that both countries could benefit under the new terms. Where are the new terms?
I quote:
The United States, which seeks flood control plus improved power development, could get early, major benefits by an altered schedule of works on the Canadian side.
Where is that change that he said was necessary if Canada's hands were not to be tied?
Under such new terms, the Mica dam would be the best project with which to begin.
That is what he said. Are we going to start on the Mica project? I would be glad to hear.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.j
Let me go on from there. I am reading everything because I do not want any portion of these words to be lost for posterity. He says:
Apart from the economic benefits such a priority offers us, Mica is also without political handicaps.
This is the first time I have ever heard of a dam that had political handicaps, but this is one dam that has. He believed that if B.C. was worth a dam it was worth a good one. That was the attitude taken. I now want to read these words:
It would appear to be completely acceptable in Washington, Ottawa and Victoria. As to the present Columbia treaty, there can be no doubt that it ties Canada's hands.
Just picture Canada's hands tied. But now we are going to approve of the treaty because the Liberal government says it is a good treaty, even though the hands are tied just as they were. It was nonsense when he said that, and, he must have known it.
Then he said:
It would flood thousands of acres of Canadian territory and it could prevent Canada from diverting the upper Kootenay into the Columbia and the Columbia into the Fraser river systems. A good deal of scenery would be ruined and Canada might be obliged to hold back flood waters which would otherwise destroy property and endanger lives in the United States.
Aren't we going to do that now? At that time they were arguing about how much the potential flood damage would be, but that is the same situation now under the protocol.
He was going to save this nation from the awful mistakes made by the Conservative government. How he saved it was to carry out the treaty and make some declarations in a protocol, which is one of explanation, in addition of course to the sale of the downstream benefits.
Then he said:
The Columbia river treaty, in its present form, gives us $64 million as a lump sum, all-time settlement for flood control.
Does he get any more under the protocol? He said we sold out Canada when we agreed to $64 million, but now we have a treaty that they are approving, and a protocol which does not change that.
Who was deceiving whom in 1961 when the Liberal party in British Columbia pretended it was going to do something with the treaty, and said it was wrong? Let me read on:
Economically speaking, the Columbia river treaty is a poor deal for Canada.
That is what he said, speaking for the Liberal party, as the chairman of the Liberal party committee; and he is the adviser of the Prime Minister today. Now they are going

to carry it out; and I ask, who was kidding whom back in 1961 during the election campaign?
We are obliged to build three storage dams costing around $400 million. The United States has to invest only $100 million in generating facilities and flood control payments to Canada. Yet the additional energy produced in the United States is split on a fifty-fifty basis.
What change is made to meet that criticism? Was that simply political deception to be practised on the people of British Columbia, or was he speaking then with the authority he has as a great engineer and economist?
Obviously Canada's share of this downstream benefit energy will cost us at least four times as much as it does the Americans.
Have they changed that? Has that been altered?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
It still costs us the same, yet we are asked to approve of that which the hon. gentleman in 1961 said was a sell-out of Canada. He then went on and said:
There is only one way of rescuing the treaty, from a short term economic point of view. That is to sell most, or all, of Canada's downstream power entitlement to the United States for cash at a price, say, of five mills per kilowatt hour.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: That is what we did.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
We endeavoured to bring about the sale, and we had all the negotiations done in that connection. That represented something that would have been achieved under the treaty in any event.
Then he went on to say:
Why, then, should Canada accept a once-and-for-all settlement for this service?
Isn't it doing it now, under the treaty and the protocol? What did the hon. gentleman mean when he wrote these words? Was he speaking with sincerity then, or has he seen the light in the change from the opposition benches to the near treasury benches? Then he said:
Why accept a lump sum payment of $64 million and be obliged to prevent flooding in the United States forever?
So that there would be no mistake that the "forever" meant forever-eternal and everlasting-it was put in italics. What change has been made in that connection? Are we not today forever accepting $64 million for flood control?
Sir, this article that I read from was used all over British Columbia to give the people an understanding of what Liberalism stood for. Then he went on:
Surely it would be much better, from a long-run point of view, to have the value of this service re-assessed year after year (as is the case with the power benefits) and flood control payments made on an annual basis.
Columbia River Treaty Why did they not do it? There is not one alteration in this connection, yet they said we had committed the unpardonable offence of selling out Canada.
Then he said what we should do:
One comprehensive plan to develop the resources of the upper Columbia in Canada has been adopted and written into the treaty. Others are possible.
What are they? Well, he said there was General McNaughton's plan:
General McNaughton, for instance, believes that Canada should immediately divert the flood waters of the upper Kootenay through Canal Flats into the Columbia. This water would then be regulated by building an additional storage reservoir in the vicinity of lake Windermere.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved:
subtopic: POLLUTION
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CREATION AT CONTROL DIVISION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of the creation of a water pollution control division, composed of representatives of the ten provinces, within the framework of the proposed national resources council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate, and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces; in addition, to further the study of water pollution control problems of a national character.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as far as the House of Commons is concerned it appears that this has been pretty much of a water week. I trust however that in discussing this motion this afternoon hon. members on the government side will not get into as much hot water as they have on the previous subject under discussion. Our party has always been very concerned with the conservation, development and proper use of natural resources, and on that account for a good number of years I moved a resolution in this house which was in the following terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of calling a dominion-provincial conference on conservation, with the view to the establishment of a nationwide policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.
I introduced that resolution every year for seven or eight years, and there was always general agreement in principle to it, but it was usually killed by time. It was talked out by government members-indeed, by members on both sides of the house, with the exception of the members of this party. I was very curious, Mr. Speaker, to find out why this was so. Everybody would appear to support the principle and purpose of the motion, yet it was talked out repeatedly year after year.

Finally I found out the reason, and I should like to quote from what Mr. Lesage had to say, when he was minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, on the motion to which I have just made reference. As reported at page 1565 of Hansard for February 27, 1956, I said of Mr. Lesage- I always like to quote myself when I find I have been correct and have accomplished something:
When speaking on my resolution last year the minister gave three reasons for not agreeing to accept it. While he supported the principles of conservation in general, he gave these three reasons for not being able to accept the resolution. First, he said that the prime responsibility for conservation of resources rests with the provincial governments. Second, he said that the suggestion for federal action should come from the provincial governments. Third, he had grave doubts as to the success of a conference called to deal with all renewable natural resources.
Now, Mr. Speaker, no doubt the change in the government of Quebec which came about with the defeat of the Duplessis regime and the election of the Liberal party in Quebec provided a more favourable climate for the consideration of such a resolution. I think that is quite true, and on that account, and-because I give credit where it is due- on account of the particular interest in natural resources of the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), the former Progressive Conservative government called the well-known conference on resources for tomorrow which lasted from October 23 to 28, 1961. I might say in this connection that there was very thorough preparation for this conference. There were three years of preparation before it was called, because I was kept informed from week to week as to just what was being done in this regard, and I think those responsible for the preparation deserve credit on that account.
The conference was held and it was a great success. People interested in all aspects of renewable natural resources were at the conference. Many worth-while papers were read. Lengthy discussions were held, and as a result of the conference several valuable reports were issued which I trust all hon. members have on their office shelves, because they are well worth referring to when one is considering the question of natural resources. Then the council of resource ministers was established as a result of this conference, a staff provided, and they are now operating. The objectives of the Canadian council of resource ministers were outlined, with which objectives I think all hon. members of the house would agree in principle.
Now I want to deal with one or two reports made by this council. In the January 20220-45
Water Pollution Control bulletin issued by the Canadian council of resource ministers the following appears:
Research team studies resource agreements.
The secretariat of the Canadian council of resource ministers has commenced a thorough review of legislation, programs and agreements affecting Canada's renewable resources.
That is all to the good.
The review is under the direction of Dr. William E. Haviland, 39, of Montreal, economist with the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association. Dr. Haviland has been granted a leave of absence from the association to co-ordinate the review activities at secretariat headquarters. The results of the review are to be submitted to the next plenary session of the council, in Charlottetown, P.E.I., this spring.
Dr. Haviland will be in charge of a research group that will study agreements directly related to renewable resources-water, land, fish, forests and wildlife-as well as agreements bearing on the multipurpose use of resources, including recreation and regional development. Members of the research team will conduct a series of meetings and interviews with government officials across the country.
The project, which was one of the main recommendations to emerge from the 1961 resources for tomorrow conference, was formally approved by the council meeting in Montreal last November.
The review will follow the principles laid down by the council. The ministers, in endorsing a review of existing agreements, also favoured the study and analysis of any new proposed programs on renewable resources. They recognized that where the federal government is party to such resource programs with one or more provincial governments, reference to the council was particularly important. They also saw an advantage in having interprovincial resource agreements submitted to the council, thus enabling the council to fulfil its desired advisory and consultative role.
Under the review, each resource agreement will be thoroughly analysed, covering such facets as the history and nature of the program, legislation, jurisdictional problems, participation of governments in preliminary studies and planning, as well as in the implementation of the agreements. Other aspects will be the application of cost-benefit analysis, education and information problems. The review team will also identify areas where new agreements might be desirable and will make specific recommendations.
What a different climate and atmosphere with respect to the joint consideration of the development of resources between the federal and the provincial governments; and that is all to the good.
Now I want to quote briefly from bulletin No. 2 for February, 1964.
Water crisis grows: Major study planned.
The crisis grows. Wells in southwestern Ontario have run dry. Drought lingers for yet another year in southeastern Alberta. The great rivers, the St. Lawrence, the Ottawa, the North Saskatchewan, the Saint John, and the great lakes, as well continue as giant receptacles for man's foul discharges. Canada's precious resource is threatened.
Across the border, ocean salt water pours into the lowering water tables supplying the city of Baltimore. New York city is forced to ration its water when the supply all but runs out. Deserts of the world now hide the remains of civilizations that disappeared with their vanishing water resource. There is world-wide concern.

Water Pollution Control
Canada, despite the fact that it is blessed with one quarter of the world's fresh water supply, finds her stocks which are readily available to her people, being rapidly depleted through neglect, mismanagement and lack of knowledge. The senior governments are now preparing to meet the situation. The first step will be to acquire complete knowledge of the water resource, the very basis of proper management of water as a vital element of the human environment.
Knowing of the purposes of the Canadian council of resource ministers and its particular interest at this time in the state of our water pollution problems, I think that my motion is most appropriate in purpose and in timing. The need for action to deal with the problem of pollution is known. It is known all across Canada by intelligent people who have given any consideration to the question. It is also known to the people of Kootenay West who are becoming increasingly concerned about the possibility of the pollution of the Kootenay and Columbia rivers because of the increase of population, the increased discharge of sewage into these rivers and the undoubtedly extensive pollution that will occur from the building of the high Arrow dam on the Arrow lakes if it is ever built.
Time and time again when you pick up the newspapers you find references to this question. In the Globe and Mail of June 27, 1963 there is an article headed "More Suds" which reads in part as follows:
Is the froth caused by detergents' refusal to break down in sewage treatment just unsightly, or is it a major factor in pollution?
In the Globe and Mail of June 29, 1963 there is an article headed "A Shocking Forecast", reading in part as follows:
A shocking forecast of the pollution threatening the streams and rivers in this area has been made by the metropolitan regions conservation authority.
In the Globe and Mail of May 29, 1963 another article appears headed "Welland River Study Seeks Way to Control Pollution and Erosion". Then there was a very interesting article in the Globe and Mail of May 18,	1963, headed "Ontario's Squandered
Water", reading in part as follows:
The province has plenty of water but industrial and civic pollution leaves much of it not fit to use.
In my own local paper I read this headline: "Association of Kootenay Municipalities Delegates Have Hot Debate on Pollution". I also read an article on a later meeting in which the pollution control program of British Columbia with respect to our own district is being criticized, and there is evidence of demands for co-operation between all levels of government.
The problem is thoroughly known so there is no necessity for me to give further illustrations of the crying need. I propose this

motion because effective action to meet this long standing and growing problem depends on a number of things. First of all, I have moved this motion in its present terms because we in this party believe that effective action depends on co-operative action between all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. Very little has been done in that respect to date. The problem requires cooperation between government research institutions and university research institutions to find out the facts and how we should deal with the problem. It needs the co-ordination of the administrative services of all levels of government and all other agencies established by other organizations and people to deal with this question. It needs a clear definition of the objectives that we seek to meet the problem in Canada as a whole. It also needs a good education program.
While people are generally concerned about the problem if they come into direct contact with and are immediately affected by some particular type of pollution, there are many people who are unaware of the hazard it presents to health and happiness in Canada at this time. We also require publicity. I have always been one who believes that the value of our natural resources and the necessity to conserve them should be taught in our schools. Our children should be brought up from at least the senior grades of the elementary schools and right through the high schools to appreciate what we have in Canada, so far as natural resources are concerned, and our responsibility for their proper conservation and development. This will require satisfactory press releases and articles in magazines. I also suggest there should be action on the part of those persons in governments responsible for health and welfare. I am very glad to see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) is listening to me carefully because such persons should take every opportunity to inform the people of what governments are doing about the problem, and of the need for co-operation between all levels of government and on the part of the people themselves.
I am not going to speak at length. I want to give other members an opportunity to speak on this motion because I know there are a number on both sides of the house who are interested. In my opinion the passing of this motion this afternoon would indicate that this house recognizes the need for co-operative action now. Second, it would demonstrate to the Canadian council of resource ministers our concern, and that we are looking to them to take action along the lines proposed in this motion. Third, I think it would provide an opportunity for the participation in the very near future of all levels of government

and, as I have said before, all research institutions and all administrative bodies, and the people of Canada, working together to tackle a problem that grows worse daily.

speechtext:
I am quite aware that the resources for tomorrow conference in 1961 proposed that an intergovernmental study be made of pollution. All I am saying in answer to the hon. member is that there exists today a permanent secretariat under the Canadian resource ministers council which, in our view, has the necessary staff and the necessary qualifications to initiate a study of the matter of water pollution, and that we need not set up a new board to do it.
I believe all hon. members of the house share with the hon. member his feeling that the pollution of our water, of our air and even of our soil is everybody's business today, and that it knows no municipal boundaries or provincial boundaries. Without going into some of the facts that are disturbing more and more people, I might say that a recent study contained in a magazine entitled "Civic 20220-45J
Water Pollution Control Administration" outlined a number of alarming facts. It appears that the great lakes, with the possible exception of certain parts of lake Superior, are already polluted, and that includes the St. Lawrence river as well. The Ottawa river is polluted from this national capital right down to the point where it joins with the St. Lawrence. The Red river, especially in its lower reaches, also is heavily polluted. Many of the waters surrounding Vancouver island and the waters about the city of Vancouver such as English bay right out to Spanish banks, are also polluted.
Domestic sewage and industrial wastes are the two main causes of pollution that have been added recently to new agricultural wastes in the form of pesticides which may one day constitute just as serious a menace to the people of this country. It may be of interest to the house to know that in the United States today industrial wastes from the food processing industry and from the pulp and paper industry have added more to the pollution problem than all the domestic sewage in the United States. I imagine the same situation obtains in Canada.
It has been estimated, too, that only 20 per cent of Canadian municipalities have adequate sewage treatment schemes. I would say that the seriousness of the problem, certainly in some areas of the country, has reach-reached proportions that are beyond the range of the municipal level and, in certain cases, even beyond the range of the provincial level, when we talk about industrial wastes which are dumped into interprovincial rivers. Despite the efforts of certain industrial and private organizations to control pollution, the complexity of the various situations in which water pollution is found, the conflicts in jurisdiction, the conflict between the public and private sectors in the use of water, have made this problem difficult to solve.
We have also had unfortunate situations in which provinces, dealing with their interprovincial rivers, have considered the selfinterest of the province rather than the interest of a neighbouring province. These competing self-interests have not been reconciled. Perhaps the principal reason public moneys have not been directed in sufficient amounts to meet this problem is that, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said, we have until recently been faced' with public apathy over the hazards to the men, women and children of this country, which come from the continued pollution of our natural waters.
What the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources proposes to do is to refer the whole subject matter of pollution to the Canadian council of resource ministers. He intends to write a personal letter to each of

Water Pollution Control the ten provincial ministers of natural resources suggesting that the question of pollution be given to the permanent secretariat of this council now functioning in Montreal. The suggestion will be that pollution be put on the agenda for the next plenary session of the Canadian council of resource ministers which is to be held, as the house knows, in Prince Edward Island on June 22 and 23 of this year.
Now, that being so, perhaps I might just outline why we feel this is the proper body to study the subject, and why it is a good idea. The hon. member for Kootenay West brought the house up to date on what the permanent secretariat of the Canadian resource ministers council has been doing. It is a new co-operative body composed of the ten provincial representatives and of the federal government, and is an example in practice of co-operative federalism. The purpose of this body is to study the varied problems relating to Canada's multiple use resources, based on the principle of equal participation between the ten provinces and the federal government. The chairmanship of this organization is on a rotating basis. The chairman this year is the Hon. Rene Levesque, who is minister of natural resources in the province of Quebec. When the chairmanship changes hands in the spring of this year it will go to Mr. Rossiter of Prince Edward Island, and subsequently to Mr. Williston of British Columbia. The council, and its permanent secretariat, already have terms of reference wide enough to cover the study of pollution. The council, and the secretariat, are to provide for a continuing examination of resource agreements and to serve as a forum for the continual exchange of views in respect of resource development policies, and programs to stimulate public interest in the multiple use resources; to organize meetings and conferences on renewable resources. It is, as well, a clearing house of information and a centre of information.
There are certain advantages I will suggest to the house in having this matter of pollution referred immediately to the Canadian council of resource ministers. The first is that this is a unique forum whereby discussions at the plenary session are at the ministerial level. The ministers responsible to their provinces and the federal Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources are in a position to make decisions and implement them at the policy level. This is the forum, because of this ministerial representation, in which to develop more consistent water pollution control legislation, consistent from one end of the country to the other. In this way, we will not have various provincial acts at loggerheads with each other.

Since pollution and the use of water resources is, except in so far as it relates to interprovincial rivers, a provincial matter, the federal government as an equal partner with the provinces in the council is in a position, through the council, to suggest a means of co-ordinating a water resources program for the entire country. I say, too, that this Canadian council of resource ministers, which is in its infancy as the hon. member for Kootenay West will appreciate, and has as its sole concrete work at the moment the review of resource agreements across the country, needs a subject of immediate public interest in order to capture public imagination. The subject of pollution would do that. I would think that if the ministers for the provinces accept the suggestion of my minister and put this matter of pollution on the agenda for the June meeting, the objective the house would want to achieve, of getting a pollution policy for the whole country, to protect our people from the contamination of our waters, our air and our soil, would be achieved.
