speechtext:
First, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on his determination, on his insistence, in bringing back to the house time and again suggestions for coping with the pollution problems of Canada. The notice of motion brought down by this private member is, of course, in precisely the same words as it was last year when this issue was debated on July 8, 1963.
The hon. member believes that we need to create another division or department to control pollution. He has also felt, in the past, that amending the Criminal Code by providing for heavier fines would solve most of the pollution problems which face us in this country. He may be right. However, I feel we already have enough divisions, department and boards, both international, federal and provincial which are geared to the study and control of pollution and which have sufficient information with regard to pollution. I feel, also, that we already have many laws concerning pollution. I do not intend to go once again into the details of these propositions by naming the various departments or citing the laws, because I did so in the course of the debate on the same motion last year and I believe it would be wasting the time of the house to repeat what is already on record in Hansard. However, if any hon. members are interested they can find this information on page 1945 of Hansard, volume two, of the 1963 session.
The problem of pollution, Mr. Speaker, is the concern of every Canadian and it should be on the list of priorities here, in the House of Commons. Canada is blessed with an abundance of natural resources, and one of our main resources is our fresh water supply. The great lakes system is the largest body of fresh water in the world. We have in Canada, in our midst, one quarter of the world's fresh water supply. Yet despite the many laws and acts which have been passed by parliament, by provincial governments and other authorities to prohibit pollution, we have allowed, and are still allowing, the wholesale pollution of our beautiful lakes and rivers.
In this connection, I was amazed by what I read in an article published in the December 1963 edition of the Reader's Digest under the heading "Valencia's Tribunal of Waters". Valencia is the third largest city in Spain, and this court was created, it is suggested, around the year 960 during the Arab occupation by the caliphs, to administer the ancient Arab laws concerning water. There is no written clause in any law or constitution in Spain which warrants the existence of such a court. The tribunal has existed for over

1,000 years, from generation to generation, by the sanction of tradition. The court, which is the oldest in Europe, meets every Thursday in the open air, outside the cathedral, to pass judgment on anyone found guilty of polluting or misusing the waters of the river Turia and its eight irrigation canals.
The people of this area have been concerned about their precious water supply for over 1,000 years. From the verdict of their court there is no appeal. Those summoned before the tribunal include builders, businessmen, municipal officers and farmers. For example, a soft drink distributor is fined $150 for letting into a canal the water in which his bottles have been washed. Mayors of municipalities are summoned if any of their citizens use the canals for sewage disposal. A soap factory is fined $650 for contaminating a canal with its residue; a farmer is fined for allowing his cattle to pass through the water; another for allowing cuttings from trees to float down it, or for washing vegetables in it, and so on. Yet the cost of running this court amounts to no more than $550 a year.
Here in Canada we have many laws concerning pollution, but no one dares to take the guilty to court for fear of incurring heavy costs

the costs occasioned by appeal after appeal, which no individual can afford. Both federal and provincial authorities have failed to enforce the laws which come under their jurisdiction. The guilty parties in Canada are, for the most part, municipalities and industries and, as for taking them to court, it should be understood that in many cases they have received permission from health departments of their respective provinces to dump untreated sewage and effluent into our streams.
In his motion which we are debating today, the hon. member for Kootenay West has asked for the creation of a water pollution control division. I would again point out to the house that, in my view, we do not need another division or department to tell us that the Ottawa river, lake St. Louis or the waters around the island of Montreal are polluted. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you as I did on July 8 last, that the solution of the pollution problem involves strictly financial considerations. I suggest that this government should offer to share jointly in the provision of funds to deal with it on the basis of one third to be paid by the government of Canada, one third by provincial governments and one third by municipal governments. As to industrial pollution along our rivers, the arrangements should be on the basis of one third to be paid by the gov-one third from provincial funds and one third from industry itself. Only as a result

of a serious program of financial responsibility will we be able to make our rivers clean again, and I suggest that the present government take up this matter at the provincial conference to be held this April and, also, that consideration of pollution problems be given priority at the meetings of the Canadian council of resource ministers to be held on June 22 and 23 of this year.
As to the motion itself, I cannot agree with the suggestion that another division or department be formed. I do feel, however, as does the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) that the secretariat and the staff of the resource ministers council should be the body responsible for collecting and evaluating all information from across Canada and for working in co-operation with the national research council to develop scientific methods of purification. The members of the resource ministers council are cabinet ministers in their respective governments and it is they, in turn, who should make the proper decisions on policy governing the introduction of new laws, financial responsibility and financial participation. I was happy to hear from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that the minister intends to take action in this regard.
The Ottawa river which, mainly as a result of pollution by industrial waste and municipal sewage is, I believe, the most polluted river in Canada, is an interprovincial river. For this reason its condition is the responsibility of the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario, the federal government, the various municipal governments and of the industries along its banks. These polluted Ottawa waters empty into the clear St. Lawrence river at lake St. Louis, adding seriously to pollution there. Of course, many of the municipalities on the island of Montreal, including the city of Montreal, dump untreated raw sewage into the St. Lawrence, also adding seriously to the pollution there. The oxygen content of the water thereby is depleted, in consequence of which all aquatic life and waterfowl are harmed. Human health and human life are eventually affected because these conditions give rise to contagious diseases and infection. In other words, this pollution eventually affects both human life and wildlife. It causes the discontinuation of the operation of beaches and park recreational facilities on river shores, and forces many municipalities, associations, and private citizens to build swimming pools which are, at times, detrimental to health when they become overcrowded or when not operated properly.
What I cannot comprehend is the fact that the newspapers will build up news to headline proportions regarding many unimportant
Water Pollution Control questions and answers dealt with in this house or will give some Canadian demagogue, who is rocking his own boat and trying to convince the population that there is a storm out at sea, a million dollars' worth of publicity about nothing. Yet when we speak and try to do something about this most important issue, pollution, which is a problem of health, a problem which touches our supply of fresh water which is necessary to life, a problem which touches every Canadian, the newspapers of this country usually remain silent. In fact, during the question and answer period the press gallery is full to capacity, but as we now talk about pollution there is only one member of the press in the gallery.

Mr. Speaker, I assure you that it is not my intention to talk out this motion. However, I do want to say'-and I appreciate the opportunity of saying it-that I am not so much interested in the technicalities of responsibility here, and as to whether it is the water pollution control division or some other agency that is charged with responsibility in this connection. It is the principle involved that is important. May I say it is my sincere belief that the majority of the people of Canada do not recognize the seriousness of the situation. They see their lakes, creeks and rivers and they think the water flows forever. Perhaps it does. But I do believe that the members of the House of Commons should be cognizant of the seriousness of the situation, because although the waters may flow, the important thing is, what is the freshness of the water for human consumption and for industry?
I had the privilege of being a member of the Canadian delegation at the NATO parliamentary conference in 1961 and I was honoured by being named a member of the special committee on scientific and technical matters. I have never forgotten the three days I spent on that committee. What was one of the major matters that was brought to our attention and discussed? It was the matter of fresh water. We, on the scientific and technical committee, were told in Paris in 1961 that in 25 years there would be a major problem throughout the world, and especially on the North American continent, with regard to the supply of fresh water.
Two European countries and the United States in particular were concerned about this problem, so much so that the United States delegate informed us that within the next 25 years his country would be facing the most serious crisis they have ever faced if they could not find an adequate supply of fresh water. This situation has arisen because water is being polluted, not only by humans but by industry itself. You can have all the water flowing that you wish, but unless it is fresh industry cannot function, nor can human life. That is why in Paris in 1961 the United States said they would make available to every country in the world all their studies on how to make fresh water out of ocean water. So far no country has found a method to do this which is reasonable in price. It is all very well for my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to introduce this motion year after year. He reintroduces this principle and expounds his concern-which, by the way, is the concern of the greatest scientists in the world and of the majority of governments in the world-regarding what

will happen to fresh water in the next quarter of a century. But it is not good enough for this House of Commons to be kind, to agree and say, "Let us refer it somewhere." Sir, the time has come-as a matter of fact, it is now long past-when we should be doing something about solving the problem of the pollution of our waters in Canada because, as was said in a previous debate, in a few years water on this continent will be worth more than gold. Now is the time for us to take care of this problem.
I sincerely hope that hon. members will not deal with technicalities and will not worry about which body should consider this problem, but will support this session in the House of Commons the principle that we recognize the problem and are going to do something about eliminating the pollution of our waters, so that those who come after us shall have fresh water, as had those who went before us. Most certainly our forefathers had better water than we have.

Mr. Speaker, before the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) speaks may I have a few moments. I agree with my colleague from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) that perhaps not too much more need be said about the treaty, but there are one or two facts which should be placed on the record first-at least, I presume they must be considered as facts.
The other night we had quite an argument in this chamber as to the relative importance of the areas which were to be flooded by the two proposals which have been under consideration by the members of the house. I have in my hand a memorandum with respect to the effect on agriculture of the construction of reservoirs on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers between Luxor and Dorr, produced by the Department of Agriculture on July 14, 1960. It says:
The building of a reservoir on the Kootenay and Columbia rivers from Luxor south to the Dorr damsite would flood some 91,000 acres of land. Of this 24,000 acres, if reclaimed, is arable without irrigation, but only some 2,800 acres of river bottom soil, all in the Kootenay basin, are used at present, primarily for the production of tame hay in association with summer cattle grazing on the uplands. About 40 farmers are involved. The remainder of the 24,000 acres would require very costly reclamation to make it usable.
There are also some 26,000 acres of land in the flooded area with some agricultural potential if irrigation could be provided. The availability and cost of utilizing water from the Kootenay, however, makes this virtually impractical for the low priced crops which could be raised in the area.
In comparison to this there are some 300,000 acres of land in the area, above the level of the reservoir, which is as potentially arable with irrigation as
Columbia River Treaty
the 26,000 acres in the reservoir area. If the reservoir water could be provided for irrigation the reservoir, in fact, increases the agricultural potential of the area.
If the building of the reservoir resulted in the control of flooding of the Columbia above Luxor an additional 20,000 to 30,000 acres of arable land in the Columbia flats, which cannot now be used because of flooding, could be made available.
So that would seem in the opinion of the Department of Agriculture at least to settle that particular argument.
I also have in my hand a letter from a retired colonel from the U.S. army corps of engineers, who incidentally and rather interestingly is a member of the Order of the British Empire. He writes from Sacramento in California because he spent a very large part of his youth in the Arrow lake country, and some of his maturity too. He says that since he was raised on the Arrow lakes he might like to comment on the provisions of this proposed treaty, and he writes:
My analysis was made on the basis of the proposed terms of the treaty as published in the Nelson Daily News, the federal power commission News Digest, and the California-Pacific northwest interconnection stage 1 progress report.
There are two compelling reasons for additional storage on the upper Columbia river, one based on engineering economics, the other political. Additional storage to firm power capacity on the lower Columbia is popular and there appears to be a growing conviction in the minds of top level Canadian and United States officials that such storage dams are right and economic, per se, just because many are economic, and because they are a step towards the large, the glamorous and the spectacular.
From the engineering economic viewpoint, the upper storage may be right and proper if the economic benefits are equal to, or greater than, the costs. If not, they cannot be justified. There may be occasions (and this appears to be one) where political expediency will magnify marginal benefits out of all proportion to their worth, in an effort to justify an otherwise uneconomic international agreement. However, the success or failure of such magnification does not prove or disprove economic justification, it merely serves to obscure engineering economics. If successful and if the costs are carefully hidden the success may add some glamour to giant storage systems and power pools, while the property owners along the Arrow lakes take the beating. Also, the public will be denied the right to enjoy one of the most scenic and most beautiful natural lakes yet untouched by a questionable economic power philosophy.
This letter is signed by Lieutenant Colonel George Anthony of the United States army, a registered professional engineer writing from Sacramento in California. He can have no particular axe to grind, except the axe of one who has lived in the Arrow lakes country and regrets to see it being destroyed under terms which he as a professional engineer does not think are justified.
In looking over the debate of the other night I was interested in the suggestions which were made by various members as to what could be done under the terms of this

Columbia River Treaty treaty. One that rather startled me was the suggestion by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) that this treaty when ratified may be of such a precarious nature that the President of the United States can knock a piece out of it when he feels like it under terms of United States legislation.
Another thing that has come out in this debate without doubt, and this is what makes it such an interesting if rather ironic debate, is that this treaty is an embarrassment to the present government and an embarrassment to the official opposition. Only one man in this house has made the slightest attempt to get them off the hook, and that was the bad boy of the Conservative party cast into outer darkness by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), the former minister of national defence. Certainly no member of the house has a better and more well deserved reputation for frankness, and the hon. member for Calgary North told the house quite bluntly and frankly that he knew, as did the government and as did the official opposition, that this was the second best treaty and that the only reason it was signed was that the premier of British Columbia held a gun to the heads of two successive governments.
I am at a loss to understand why Conservative and Liberal members of the house continue to fight a losing battle with logic, shall I say, to make out that a poor treaty is a good one, but apparently they are afraid of the premier of British Columbia. I suppose we British Columbians may stick our chests out and say that our premier has kept the government scared in the same way he had the former government scared; but I think this is a very serious matter. Anyone who knows anything about the international rivers act knows that while the federal government can stop a provincial government from doing something it considers is not in the national interest, it is quite incapable of making that provincial government adopt what is in its opinion a more suitable scheme. Mr. Bennett in his characteristic manner took full advantage of this situation and said in effect to each government in Ottawa: The Columbia will be developed on our terms or it will not be developed at all, and they both turned tail and ran.
I suggest that when we are looking for instances in which the government of Canada has been submitting to provincial pressures and when we are asked to consider a certain provincial government as being separatist and out to destroy confederation, perhaps it would do no harm if sometimes we would turn our eyes westward instead of eastward.

This particular treaty now before the house is a fine example of that. As I say, I am at a loss to understand why the present government and the official opposition have been willing to sit here day after day, under an imputation either of dishonesty or imbecility, instead of pointing the finger directly at the man who is responsible for the situation. I hope that in the hearings before the committee we shall be able to make very clear who is the prime culprit in this affair. I am afraid that neither the Liberal government nor the former Conservative government can be exonerated from cowardice, but certainly I think we shall be able to exonerate them from dishonesty and treachery with regard to the national welfare by placing the blame where it should so rightly be placed.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in closing this debate I think I should observe that we have had four days of useful discussion on a matter which was referred to by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) as one of the most important brought before this house in recent years.
In commenting within the limits of the time at my disposal on some of the points that have been made on the treaty, the protocol and related documents, I should at once speak eulogistically of those public servants of our country who over a period of many years have contributed so much to the consideration and the finalization of this matter. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) made what I thought were unnecessary, disparaging remarks about certain public servants in Canada. In fairness to the hon. gentleman, he did try to correct the impression which in the initial stages he had created. But lest there be any doubt, I should like to say that I am sure all of us, wherever we sit in this house, would not regard it as part of our assignment in the espousal of any cause, to include, in criticism of the administration, any acts of any of our public servants.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: It may be necessary on occasion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that in this case Canada was never better served by the officials in the office of the Privy Council, in the Department of External Affairs, the engineers in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the officials of the Department of Justice, others in the government service of

Canada, and public servants from the province of British Columbia, all of whom dedicated themselves with commendable zeal to the prosecution of the matters assigned to them by their respective governments. I have more confidence in the officials of our country than apparently has the hon. gentleman, who should try to overcome the illusion that all Americans are ten feet high and that their Canadian counterparts are dwarfs.
The hon. member for Kootenay West asked a number of questions. He asked for the details of the calculations used to arrive at the figure of $64.4 million for flood control, and the additional four payments for emergency operations during the 60 years from ratification. I simply ask my hon. friend to read pages 143 and 150 of the white paper where he will find the calculations for which he has asked, and others as well. The white paper was supplied to the membership of the house before the debate began in order to refresh the minds of hon. members on some of the important facts involved in this complicated and important project.
The speaker who just took his seat referred to the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness). The hon. member for Calgary North made a serious study of this matter as a member of one of the cabinet committees in the former administration. I disagree with the hon. gentleman when he says that this is the second best possible deal that Canada could have obtained, but I do agree with the hon. member when he says that it was important to bear in mind the wishes of the province, the owner of the resource, as a consideration in the decision that the government of Canada was to reach in its negotiations with the government of the United States.
I believe that this is not the second best deal that we could reach. This is the best deal which, after a period of protracted negotiation, we could arrive at with the United States. I prefer to remind the hon. gentleman of what the hon. member for Calgary North said in concluding his observations. He said, as found on page 644 of Hansard:
Instead of spending a great deal of time now dealing with what the advantages of the Mc-Naughton plan were, I think we would be much better off to address ourselves to the realities of the situation and deal with the only plan on which it was possible to get agreement.
I believe that is the point which all of us might well bear in mind as we give consideration to this important matter.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of the membership of this house believes that the treaty, the protocol, the agreement with the province of British Columbia and the conditions of sale, represent an equitable deal for both countries and constitutes a project 20220-46i
Columbia River Treaty worthy of the name and honour of this country. It is a project which takes into account our national interests, and takes into account also the needs of our neighbours. It is a project which takes into account the availability of power now and for the future, and the means by which this great Columbia river can be harnessed for the purpose of providing energy to the people of Canada as well as to the people of the United States.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Put that the other way around.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "Put that the other way around". I would be glad to put it that way, too. I find that often, if you are prepared to recognize that others have rights as well as yourself, you are apt to get a far better agreement. This is one of the reasons we were able to conclude an agreement with the United States, after a long period of negotiation.
I have sought to deal with this matter objectively. I gave credit to all who have had anything to do with the project. I made the observation, and I repeat it, that the treaty signed by the former government in January, 1961, was basically a good treaty. And what we have done is to make it a better treaty. The evidence of this fact is embodied in the protocol and in the other supporting documents.
Now, when the right hon. gentleman spoke this afternoon he spent most of his time attacking the protocol. He attacked its alleged insufficiency. He pointed out that it did not do as much as its authors suggested. This was his argument as well as the argument of some other hon. members of his party who have supported generally the position he has taken, but who have affirmed that they are going to support the protocol as well as the treaty. Most of the right hon. gentleman's remarks today, however, were levelled at one particular member of this house, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis).

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: And against government policy before the election.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: I want to say this, that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, who was a very valuable member of the negotiating team-

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Mr. Williston says he was not on the team.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
-has rendered very distinguished service to Canada during the negotiations conducted since this government came into office. The right hon. gentleman may be interested in his discarded opinions. I must say that I feel, in singling out the hon. member for Coast-Capilano for

Columbia River Treaty special criticism today, the right hon. gentleman merely affirmed the real contribution this hon. member made to this problem generally. In doing so he also affirmed by implication, his support, as announced at the end of his speech, for the treaty, for the protocol, for the supporting documents and for the efforts of the present administration to reach a successful conclusion in the negotiations with the United States.
Today the right hon. gentleman asked us what was new in the present government's action? He said he thought the treaty was a good one but that the protocol did not represent the kind of improvements which warranted the characterizations of it by its protagonists. The right hon. gentleman forgot today, however, to recognize that the main accomplishment of the new government was to get things moving again last May, after they had been more or less stalled since the signing of the treaty in 1961. I affirm again the contribution made by the previous administration in this matter. I have not withdrawn what I said in the initial stage, and I do not withdraw it tonight. I think that what the former government did was commendable. What we did was to improve the former government's efforts through the addition of the protocol, which we were able to conclude in agreement with the United States.
One of the reasons for the improvement has not been noted by the right hon. gentleman. The fact is, we are now discussing a proposal to send the treaty and the protocol to the external affairs committee for examination. This represents a great achievement of the present administration. This is something that was not done by the former government. I say, with some respect, it is clear from all the evidence that the administration that signed the treaty in 1961 was apparently divided within itself on the question of whether or not the treaty should be pressed. It is clear that there must also have been a sharp division of opinion between the former government and the government of British Columbia, although today the right hon. gentleman said that when he signed the treaty he understood there was acquiescence by British Columbia in what the federal government was going to do.
Why there was no agreement concluded between the former government and the government of British Columbia, in a formal sense, it is difficult to understand. One of the first things we did when we undertook to try to bring about some improvement in the treaty was to get a clear, unambiguous agreement with the government of British Columbia. The fact that we were successful in doing this is shown by the two instruments which are now

part of the record of this house, contained in the white paper. We were able to get an agreement that set out the obligations of British Columbia to Canada, the obligations of Canada to the United States, the obligations which British Columbia would covenant to assume in respect of the covenants which Canada entered into with the United States. This agreement was stated in clear and unambiguous terms so that when we were dealing with the United States we knew exactly where we stood with the province of British Columbia. This is one thing that does represent an improvement in what this administration has accomplished as compared with the course followed by the previous administration headed by the right hon. gentleman.
The completion of precise and firm agreements between the federal government and the provincial governments prepared the way for the final negotiations with the United States and ultimately, we hope and believe, for ratification of the treaty. There was no indication whatever that the previous government was contemplating, or could make, the kind of arrangement with the province of British Columbia which was essential for progress in this matter. That is clear.
What is the situation before us now? We were able to conclude a protocol with the United States and we were able to get an agreement from the United States as to the compensation to be paid for the sale of the downstream power benefits. What is new in what this government has done? We were able to get a covenant from the United States in the form of a treaty obligation to pay to Canada for the benefit of British Columbia a sum of money that will more than take care of the total cost of all the three storages, and that will provide a surplus in addition to the amount required for the payment of the cost of the storages.
In addition, we were able to be assured that, as a result, there could be generated at one of the dams, at Mica, power available to Canadian consumers in British Columbia at a rate that will compare with that available anywhere in Canada. Those are some of the new features which are the result of the successful negotiations by the present administration with the government of the United States.

speechtext:
Would the Secretary of State for External Affairs permit a question? If the government of the United States or the United States authority is to make a lump sum payment for the downstream power, and this payment is to be made into the foreign exchange counter fund and is locked up in long term investment, and in order to pay money to the

province of British Columbia to meet the expenses of building dams the government of Canada will have to borrow money-I assume at a substantial interest rate-how then will there be an accumulation of interest and an accumulation in the capital fund to that level which the minister says will be attained?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is a question we will go into very carefully in the committee. My hon. friend has asked me a question, and though he has taken me off the main nature of my reply, I should like to tell him that the lump sum will be paid to Canada in United States dollars, and Canada will add these funds to its exchange resources.
The United States funds will then be invested in U.S. short or medium term government securities, as is the custom with foreign exchange reserves, and will be held by Canada in this form until needed. To suit the convenience of the U.S. balance of payments, the securities in question will be nonmarketable. U.S. government securities of a rather longer maturity than is usual, but will be reasily redeemable in cash as and when needed by Canada.
Canada will pay to British Columbia the corresponding amount of the lump sum payment, in Canadian dollars. Such funds will be paid from the consolidated revenue fund, as in the case for any other addition to Canadian exchange resources. The result will be that British Columbia will receive the Canadian equivalent of the U.S. payment almost simultaneously with the payment by the U.S. The actual transfer through the banking system in Canada may take several weeks to complete, in view of the large amount involved. That is the answer to my hon. friend's question.
There is no doubt about it that we have a project that will enable us to develop the Columbia river as a result of an agreement made with the United States, under which that country will pay for the cost of the storages, thus making it possible for British Columbia to supply power at Mica at 1.5 mills, a rate that is comparable with almost any other resource in terms of this particular form of energy available to Canada.
That is what the protocol, in part does. Yet the right hon. gentleman says that all we have done was to provide certain minor clarifications to a treaty which we admit was basically sound. Not only have we taken a treaty that was basically sound and given it effectiveness, but we have been able to arrive at a clear agreement with the province of British Columbia concerning our respective obligations.
When the right hon. gentleman signed the treaty in 1961 he had no idea as to price.
Columbia River Treaty He had no idea as to what compensation was going to be paid to British Columbia for the sale of the downstream benefits. He had no idea what was going to be the convenant or contractual arrangement between the government of British Columbia and the government of Canada. One may well ask how any government would enter into a treaty with another sovereign power unless there were clear understandings on these very points.
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman said that the protocol which we concluded did not really cover fundamental considerations. When we get into the committee stage we will be able to examine this statement of the right hon. gentleman. We will be able to examine the protocol. We will be able to see whether or not the modifications and the clarifications that we achieved were in Canada's interest. I am sure that the protocol negotiated by this government, in close and constructive co-operation with the province of British Columbia, has provided a more satisfactory basis for proceeding with the arrangements with the United States.
I have already set out the main points of the protocol on pages 473 to 476 of Hansard for March 3. An examination of that protocol will reveal that we were able to reach with the United States not merely clarifications, not merely adjustments or modifications and improvements. The fact emerges that the treaty with the protocol provides a better basis than existed before for going ahead with ratification.
For example, no one will deny, on examination, that the power benefits contemplated by the treaty have been improved by very substantial amounts as a direct result of points established in the protocol. The change in the stream flow basis has increased Canada's energy benefits by about 18 per cent. The provision regarding pumping requirements at Grand Coulee has added between 5 per cent and 7 per cent to Canada's capacity credit.
The provisions in paragraphs 5 and 7 of the protocol regarding operation of storages in Canada and at Libby certainly produce a much better situation from Canada's point of view than most of the earlier critics had thought was possible on the basis of the provisions of the treaty itself.
On flood control many of the more serious critics of the original treaty had deplored the high degree of control apparently given to the United States without any checks or restraints. The protocol gives Canada a substantial voice in flood control and it also establishes objective standards for determining when additional flood control can be called for. These are all real improvements.

Columbia River Treaty
Several of the points in the treaty which had provoked criticisms among the lawyers have been straightened out in the protocol. This is particularly true concerning the matter of precedents, diversions and the status of the boundary waters treaty.
Today, the right hon. gentleman asked what the protocol had done with regard to the right of diversion. He said the protocol had simply confirmed what was already in the treaty with regard to the right of diversions for consumptive uses to assist the prairie lands in terms of necessary irrigation.
I do not deny that this is a fact, but to state it in the way in which the right hon. gentleman stated it is to give a wrong impression. There was thought to be some ambiguity in article XIII(l) of the treaty as to the right of diversion for consumptive use. Lawyers might interpret that clause in different ways. Some would say it did not give an absolute right in terms of consumptive use as seemingly was intended in article XIII of the treaty signed by the right hon. gentleman. I was one of those who did not share that view. I thought the article was clear. But there were some who thought that was not the situation. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) was among them.

The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) the other day-

The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, in what I thought was a most thoughtful speech on the disposition of the power which will result from the undertaking, said as reported at page 491 of Hansard:
We are going to sell power which we are told will be available at a cost of approximately 1.5 mills. That is the lowest cost power, I suspect, in the whole of Canada, let alone British Columbia, and we are going to see all of it in the United States. Why?
This was the question asked by the hon. gentleman and, as I say, he made one of the most thoughtful speeches of this debate. I should like to point out to him that the power which Canada will have available at less than 1.5 mills is not the power which is to be sold to the United States. That is the power which is to be developed at Mica-

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Delivered in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
There is nothing in any of the documents before the house to suggest the sale of that power. The power which is being proposed for sale is the downstream benefits produced at United States generators. That is the power for which Canada will be paid $274.8 million.
I am paying some attention to the remarks made by the hon. member because I think this is a very important point and one which is of real interest to the people of British Columbia. He said, further:
I think the people of British Columbia are entitled to know whether they are going to get this Peace river power, which is supposed to make these downstream benefits surplus, at the same cost as the downstream benefits. Or are they going to be asked to pay 10, 12, or 14 mills for it? We want to know on what basis the government of Canada agreed with the government of British Columbia that this power is surplus to requirements.
That is a very pertinent statement which the hon. gentleman has made. I would point out to him that the cost of power from the
Columbia River Treaty Peace as estimated in 1961 by consulting engineering firms from the United Kingdom ranged between 4.2 and 4.4 mills per kilowatt hour. Since then, savings have been realized at the project and perhaps it is not unreasonable to suggest that the final price might be in the neighbourhood of four mills. What would be the cost to Canada of the downstream benefits if they were returned to Canada and sold at a price which would permit the generation of 1.5 mill power at Mica, as does the present proposal? To do that, the revenues from the sale in Canada of these downstream benefits would, in a 30 year period, have to provide for all the capital costs of the treaty storage dams, half the cost of generators at Mica, the stand-by transmission charge imposed by the treaty, and the cost of transmitting the downstream benefits from Oliver to British Columbia loads. I would note that if the power were brought back to Canada we would have no guarantee as to the amount we would get. Under the present arrangement we have a guaranteed payment and we know exactly where we stand.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) had something to say by way of criticism of the treaty. He implied that the value of the treaty would be limited to a saving in the cost of Mica generation of $16 million a year up to the year 2003. An examination of the facts alone makes it clear that this is only part of the value which Canada will receive. Not only will there in addition be a later saving at Mica of $13 million a year after the year 2003, but the whole scheme will be worth many times that amount to Canada, as was indicated in the statement I gave the other day. The $16 million represents merely the annual savings, not the full value, which will be achieved at Mica alone in each of the first 30 years. The structures that will exist and the services that will be provided to Canada, both on the Columbia and the Kootenay river, will be worth an incalculable amount over the remaining years of the treaty and subsequently.
The hon. gentleman said, as is reported at page 495 of Hansard:
-even If we get $16 million a year of benefit, that will not begin to compensate Canada for the payments that will have to be made, to people who are dispossessed from their homes and places of business, for communities that are flooded, to say nothing of the fact that it will not begin to pay for the loss of the productivity of thousands of acres of land which will be flooded in perpetuity.
I can only assume that the criticism of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in this regard concerns only the Arrow lake dam, as the other two treaty projects are included in the sequence 9A plan which he indicated

Columbia River Treaty he supports. With regard to the Arrow lake dam, over 40 per cent of the estimated total cost of the project involves expenditures on the reservoir area itself and includes such items as were referred to by the hon. member. Therefore the cost of such items is not an extra cost which will offset the advantages of the treaty.
My hon. friend went on to point out that there was an implication that the treaty would supply cheap power to the United States. For any sales agreement there must, of course, be some advantage both to the purchaser and to the seller. However, the power being purchased by the United States utilities is being purchased at a price higher than present Pacific northwest power rates. It should further be noted that the power purchased is of a diminishing quantity and therefore of less value than a continuing amount. It is also of an unknown quantity as the actual benefits received will depend upon future conditions.
The hon. gentleman said that as a result of this treaty we would find that our aluminum industry would leave British Columbia. That is not the situation indicated by the energy requirements of the aluminum industry in the Pacific northwest United States.

The aluminum industry in the northwestern United States has only been held back by a lack of abundant cheap power-
I have looked at the report of the Bonneville power administration for 1963, and that report says that "beginning with 1958 some of the aluminum plants curtailed their firm power loads". The report says, further, that in fact such curtailments in 1958 through 1963 cost the Bonneville power administration $5,500,000 in loss of revenues. As of June 30, 1963, these aluminum plants were operating at about 65 per cent of their interruptible power capacity. So there is nothing to warrant or justify the statement made by the hon. member.

and the former government of Canada, and we have made it into a better treaty, into a better arrangement for British Columbia and for Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all agree that it is desirable that there should be a special committee of the house established for the consideration of the procedure and organization of this house.
Hon. members on all sides are anxious to see parliament function in the most efficient manner possible, and we will want to examine our procedures and our rules to see whether these cannot be devised in a way to render more efficient our daily work in this house. I think it will be generally agreed that the way in which we can give consideration to this question is by the establishment of a committee in which the various points of view of the respective parties can be stated, all designed to render more efficient our operations and procedures. I think the remarks which have already been made by the right hon. gentleman on another occasion in this connection could be taken as supporting in principle what I have said, and the quicker this committee can get to work the more advantageous, I am sure, will be the result.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could use the words of the scriptures-"Almost thou persuadest me"-but I feel I ought to place
Procedure Committee
before the house some suggestions additional to those to which the minister alluded when he referred to the views I had expressed on another occasion.
I think we all compliment the Speaker on the manner in which he has acted in bringing about this select committee on procedure and organization. After all, changes in the rules of parliament have become necessary with changing times. If one reads what Burke said in the 1780's he can only conclude that parliament would never change, because he said that the instrument of parliament in its practices of that day was perfect. Again, at the time of the reform acts of 1832 the attitude of the Duke of Wellington was that the status quo should be maintained and that no changes should take place or were necessary. I think that we as a parliament have a responsibility to place before the people of Canada as a whole the fact that, while we do not always operate with the efficiency of a dictatorship, parliament maintains and assures freedom. It can never be as effective as a dictatorship in getting things done, but so long as there is a free parliament so long will freedom be maintained. Our responsibility is to ensure that this institution shall not deteriorate in the opinion of the public, much less decay because of the failure on our part to bring parliamentary procedure up to date.
The rules are generally the same as they have been for generations. There is only one change which I noticed in the parliamentary rules of 1791 and 1792 over what they are today, and that is the rule that provided that if any member failed to be in his place in the house the Speaker, on noticing his absence, would bring the absence to the attention of the sheriff who would forthwith bring that member before parliament to answer to the Speaker for his failure to be present. That rule it was found necessary to alter with the passing dates, but by and large parliamentary procedure represents the wisdom of generations and is designed, as the minister said, to bring about a full and purposeful discussion of the matters before us.
While we are all for modernizing the rules, such modernization must have full regard to the rights of minorities. Rules are designed to assure not only effectiveness in parliamentary debate but also the preservation of the rights of minorities against the power of majorities. We must ensure that freedom of discussion is not reduced unnecessarily. Having once headed a government I know very well that a government always feels that the opposition is practising obstruction; but it must be very clearly understood that in any modification of the rules recommended by the committee there shall not be any diminution in the acknowledged right of the house

Procedure Committee
to discuss fully, to criticize if it will, but above all to give the fullest consideration to measures which are brought in.
I think a reform is necessary in many of our rules. We are judged by the people as a whole by what we do here and the manner in which we discharge public business. Therefore, in the improvement of the effectiveness of our techniques we should do everything we can to make those changes which are necessary without sacrifice of the rights of parliament. Above everything else we must be careful that in any reform we introduce we do not make the cabinet more powerful than it is today. Certainly the trend in the last 40 years has been to an ever-strengthening cabinet at the expense of an ever-weakening parliament.
I have a number of suggestions, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to make in this connection. They do not begin to exhaust the matters which might come before the committee, but I think the government could do a great deal to assist the organization of business if more legislation were initiated in the Senate.
Now with regard to this house, I think that with six supply motions available in each session, with the exception of the first, which would last two days, the others might be restricted to one day. For after all, in the course of one day on a motion to go into supply there would be available to all parts of the house the opportunity to debate the amendment.
I think we should add to the time of sittings. I know this is not very popular but you cannot always be popular if you want to get effectiveness and efficiency. I should like to see the time of sittings added to, and in particular that we would sit between six and eight o'clock.
At that time private members' hour could be effective. As it is today the house starts at 2.30. Following the question period we have an hour and a half or so on matters of government business and then we go into private members' hour between five and six. Would there be any interference with private members if a similar provision were brought in as exists in the British house today? Between six and eight o'clock many members speak. Others are away having their dinner. To assure that no unfair advantage is taken of the government there is agreement that during that period of time no divisions will take place and no votes will be called. If we followed this suggestion we would gain many hours of the time of parliament for government business while not in any way sacrificing the rights of private members.
Next, there is the question of whether or not debate should take place on resolutions.

I know the purpose of debate on resolutions. The avowed purpose is that information shall be made available, but by and large I would see no great loss if there were no debate at the resolution stage.
Next, we come to the question of the government's responsibility in connection with questions. Some of the answers we have been receiving lately have been anything but complete, anything but informative, and their major quality has been the concealment of any information. We had an example of that today in the question I asked regarding refunds of the excess paid by some importers into Canada over and above 4 per cent and up to 11 per cent following the change that was made on July 8 in the budget resolutions. There is no reason why we should not be entitled to the fullest information.
We have had the same thing in the last few days from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer)-evasion, concealment, information denied to the house to which it is entitled, but which the Minister of National Defence has denied in the most cavalier manner. Again, in regard to the answering of questions I would point out, as the United Kingdom is referred to as an example of what should be done, that unstarred questions are answered in three days in the United Kingdom house. When answers are given that are not proper and are considered by the member who asked the question as being insufficient, the member has the right by notice in that behalf to raise any objection at the automatic adjournment hour of ten o'clock.
I mention this because there are some who are saying that the question period in this house is taking too long. In the United Kingdom they have an hour each day for questions, with the exception of Friday. There have been occasions in this session and in the past two or three sessions when that period of time has been exceeded in this house. If there is to be any fixing of a set period of time for the question period, members must at the same time have the right to raise the question of the inadequacy of answers or any other matter at adjournment time.
That happens in the parliament at Westminster. Adjournment takes place at ten o'clock. Some member has not received full information and he raises the question in the manner provided by the rules. Then there is up to half an hour's discussion on whatever the question is that is brought forward for consideration, following notice. All members do not have to be present. As a matter of fact, there are often only four or five or six or eight members. No quorum is required. The press gallery is not present to the same

degree that it normally is, but somehow or other the information that comes out in that half hour does occupy a considerable degree of importance in the dispatches from parliament.
I should also like to suggest that when we are talking about making parliament more efficient we should also consider making members more efficient. The library is a place that should be visited and its services utilized. Certainly there is a shortage of research facilities in our parliament. Anyone who visits Westminster will find that even while the house is in session there are often more members in the library than there are in the chamber. Whether that prevails in Ottawa I should not like to say, but I simply point out that good members must have that knowledge and research available to them that the library provides.
I should like consideration given to one other matter. In the past I have frequently stated that I was not entirely favourable to the desirability of an ombudsman. Events in the last year or two, as well as further study, have convinced me that this is something that should be given early consideration. The office might easily be established on an experimental basis to ascertain whether or not the benefits that are claimed will flow from the establishment of such an office would in fact be as indicated by its proponents.
There are many other suggestions that could be made but I am not going to do so at this hour. I do feel that no committee is of more importance than the committee on rules. The members have worked in cooperation. Many changes have been brought about. The period for debates has been limited. The time of speeches has been considerably reduced. All these objectives that have been obtained have been desirable. Further changes should be made, but only when those changes are entirely consonant with the effectiveness of the house being maintained and the rights of the minority secured.
We are judged, as I said a moment ago, by the people of our country. They ask for efficiency in the operation of this institution. They have that right. We want to assure that they shall have it, but at the same time we must maintain the sovereignty of the members of the house and the rights of each member, whatever position he may occupy in the house. I know of no better definition of parliament than that given by Quintin Hogg who recently gave up his peerage which came to him involuntarily some years ago.
In his work on parliament entitled, "The Purpose of Parliament", he says this:
Parliament resembles rather an ancient family mansion which has been lived in continuously for
Procedure Committee
a period of centuries, and has served the needs of those that have dwelt therein by constantly modifying and adding to its conveniences from generation to generation.
Later on, he says:
The whole has served the family well for generations of happy and vigorous life, but it baffles the planner to reduce its form to any single conception.
To those who live in it, it is a priceless possession not to be exchanged for anything more meritricious and unified. But those who are familiar with its history are sometimes apt to lose themselves in its winding corridors and to be surprised and trapped by floors built at different times and on separate levels.
This is the parliament of the United Kingdom and our parliament as well which has been built on the plan of Westminister and changed to meet Canadian needs. It has been altered by those who have preceded us. One of the greatest contributions made to parliament was made by a French Canadian who died just 100 years ago. I refer to Sir Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, the man who gave our country responsible government, a man whose courage and dedication to his people were exemplified by his stand in favour of the use of the French language in parliament at a time when only English was officially permitted. We would do well in this year of the one hundredth anniversary of his passing if our country paid tribute to one of the great leaders who gave so much to parliament and who, in his relationship with Baldwin, showed that understanding, that tolerance and that co-operative attitude that characterized the thinking which is the only basis for harmonious government in this country.
I welcome the setting up of this committee and hope that it will, at an early date, bring in preliminary recommendations. It has the benefit of the visit of the Speaker to the United Kingdom parliament. It has, as well, received the co-operation of the Speaker at Westminister and all the law clerks of the crown there. Suggestions were offered in the memorandum handed out to all members. I hope that in consequence not only of the committee meetings in past years, but as well any further information that has been secured, this committee will be able to bring in a series of suggestions that will make the House of Commons more effective, and more efficient in the discharge of business, and will, at the same time, maintain and scrupulously assure the freedom of the house and of the individual members.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the New Democratic party are in support of this motion to reappoint the special committee on procedure, which sat for a while during the closing weeks of the last session. I may say also that we are

Procedure Committee
a party to the all-party agreement to try and set this committee up with the least possible debate. I believe the understanding is that we can do it with one speaker from each party. I believe it is the hope of all of us that we may be able to complete this item of business before ten o'clock tonight, and I shall certainly do my best to keep my remarks short so that others can also speak and so that this goal can be achieved.
A motion of this nature, Mr. Speaker, does present one with the temptation to speak about the greatness of the institution of parliament, its greatness in the past and the greatness we feel it can achieve in our own time. However, I suspect that it is the view of members generally, and perhaps it is the view of those who are watching us, that what is wanted at this time is not a series of such speeches but rather that we turn the job over to the special committee and ask it to get down to work and come up with some suggestions that may help us to improve the job we do here on behalf of the Canadian people.
As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said, in addition to the work of the committee during the last session, we now have the advantage of Mr. Speaker's trip to the United Kingdom and the memorandum that has been prepared as a result of that visit. I think that we can very quickly get down to a real job of work. I hope that we will have the courage to look at our rules and our procedures, and suggest any overhauling where we feel it can improve our practices without doing violence to some of the things to which the Leader of the Opposition has just referred. I agree with him that we must not, in our desire to streamline things, to speed things up, lose any of that wisdom of the generations which is enshrined in our parliamentary procedure.
I feel that if we look at our procedures very carefully, even with the courage and the willingness to make drastic changes, we will discover that there is value, that there is reason to many if not most of the practices that we have in this parliament. The question period is something that comes in for a great deal of discussion, and suggestions are made as to ways in which it might be shortened. Let us not lose sight of the fact that this is probably one of the most important aspects of our parliamentary procedure. It is one of the things we have in our system here, and that they have at Westminster, which we think is an improvement over what they have in some other countries. It may be that even though it is tedious, even though the press gallery at times may find it a bit long, it may be that this is one of the periods in

parliament where problems that are of concern to the Canadian people are dealt with in the way we should be dealing with them.
Comments are sometimes made, too, about lengthy debates, about the amount of speaking that goes on in parliament. Let us not forget that discussion is the purpose of parliament. Parliament is not the government. Parliament is not the place where the bills that get passed are drafted or where the major decisions are made. This is the job of the government of the day. It is the proposals of the government that are brought before parliament, which in effect is a national forum, where 265 men and women discuss these proposals on behalf of the 20 million Canadians. Parliament is the place where we discuss the things that are of importance and are of concern to the people of Canada, and to do this is our duty. There may be times, Mr. Speaker, when it is parliament's job to talk, when it is parliament's job to discuss the matters that are before us, even at length. I think any judgments that are made upon the job we do here ought to be made on the basis of that kind of understanding as to what our function is.
Even though I am prepared to defend these various phases of our parliamentary procedure I will not take the time to discuss all of them. I will not go into the whole business of the throne speech, the budget debate, the supply motions and grievance procedures. They all have roots in history, roots in certain needs, and I think they have to be protected. At the same time I feel we must have the courage to find ways and means of making changes so that we can better apportion our time.
Our goal should not be just to shorten the session so that we can get away from Ottawa. Our goal should be that we do not waste our time on unimportant things and thus not have sufficient time to deal with important things. Therefore I hope the aim of the committee this session will be to do a job that will help parliament perform its function better, in the years that lie ahead.
The Leader of the Opposition has suggested a number of changes he thinks should be made. These should be considered, but I do not think it would be consistent with my offer to try to get this motion through tonight if I were to go into details of that kind. May I simply suggest that there will be an opportunity to look at all these proposed changes in the committee on procedure, and I hope we shall do a thorough job in that committee.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing I would like to say. It has been said before, and I suppose it has been said in every debate on parliamentary procedure that we have had

over the decades. It is that the rules cannot do it all. In the final analysis it depends upon the members. It depends on how we respect the rules and how we observe them. It depends, as a matter of fact, on an old fashioned word-discipline.
I have just as many examples in my mind as the Leader of the Opposition, and others, of faults on the government side; but there are faults on our side too, and if we are serious in our desire to improve the procedures of parliament we have to face up to the need for greater self-discipline on the part of us all.
The question period is a good example. I am very reluctant to agree to any suggestion that the question period be shortened by rule, because it seems to me that immediately that happens some important questions will not get asked by some members because they happen to belong to minor parties down at the end of the chamber. Yet something like that will come, unless we do much more to discipline ourselves as to questions we ask. The question period is important and should be used for the asking of important and urgent questions concerned with the problems of our people back home, but it is up to us to practice some self discipline in this; and the same thing applies to length of debate.
In suggesting what can be done by way of self discipline I am putting first things that ought to be done by opposition members, but it would not be natural for me to do this without suggesting something that can be done by the government side.
In the last day or so we have had an example of something on the government side which causes difficulty in the business of the house. A couple of weeks ago, in response to a question, we had an announcement from the government side as to what the priority of business would be for the weeks ensuing from the day the announcement was made. As a matter of fact the announcement was made on February 28, and about nine items were listed. We have taken the first item and disposed of it. We are now on the second item. So far so good; but today we had something interposed in that list which was not mentioned earlier, namely the budget.
If the budget is proposed I suppose there flows from that the budget debate, which takes six days, and then what happens to the items in that list that were given to us as the business of the house? Hon. members know that I have a particular interest, which is shared by many others, in the Canada pension plan. It was No. 8 on the list. We could anticipate that it would come on at a certain point, but now something else has come in ahead of it. The possibility of getting the debate on the Canada pension plan, which
Procedure Committee
we were assured we would get before the Easter recess, now grows very slim.
This is an example of poor discipline on the part of the government that is just as inimical to the procedures of parliament as is poor discipline on the part of opposition members in asking questions. If we are going to accept the proposition that we will improve parliament by practising some self discipline, then I suggest it applies to both sides of the house.
I shall not tonight develop what I suggested the other day, and I also had an opportunity to write a few words about the subject, but this same quality is one that it would be well for our observers in the press gallery to follow. Again I extend an invitation to the gallery to criticize us, as is their duty, but also to join with us in this effort to discover what the standards are that we should be living up to, and to help us to try and live up to those standards.
