speechtext:
When one does not get the applause where he wants it, apparently the way to get it is to ask for it.
I want to give one example, which I think proves my contention that changing the rules will not by itself do the job. I have lost track of the number of committees on rules and procedure over the past 20 years or so, on which I have had the privilege of being a member, but I think those hon. members who have been around here for that length of time will agree with me that the committee which made its report in 1955 did one of the best jobs of overhauling the rules of the house that has been done in recent decades.
It was a committee which met on and off for two or three years. It had excellent advice and guidance. A great deal of work was done. I remember some of the people who served on that committee who are not here now, such as Hon. Walter Harris and the former member for Kamloops, now Hon. E. Davie Fulton, and others of that calibre. We did a good job and we brought in a pretty complete overhaul of the rules, in so far as one can overhaul the rules of an on-going institution such as parliament. The proposals we made were brought in with unanimity.
As I say, the result was that we made a pretty substantial change in the rules of the

Procedure Committee
house, and we did one of the best jobs ever done in this field. That was in 1955, and I need only mention the year to indicate to hon. members what is in my mind. The next year was 1956, and we might as well not have had any rules at all when one recalls what happened in 1956.
I am trying to be fair and objective about this. Everyone knows what I think of the government's performance in 1956 in the pipe line debate. Everyone knows what happened to the rules in that period, but it is also true that we on the opposition side of the house, in our determination to use every device available to us to try and thwart what we thought the government was doing by way of violence to the procedure, deliberately extended the question period.
I do not think there is any question about that. It became a means of warfare, a means of counter attack because of what the government was doing. That was 1956; but the problem created by what had to be done then is still with us. Therefore I say that although a good job was done in revising the rules in 1955, the very next year produced a situation in which the government of the day paid scant heed to the rules, and in which the opposition had to find ways and means to try to prevent the government from doing the harm it was out to do. The result is that it has taken a long while since then to try and get parliament back on the rails.
I want to see the rules improved. I want to see changes made. I want to see time saved, in the sense that I want to see it apportioned better. I think the committee we are appointing can do a job for parliament and a job for Canada, but even after that is done the real success of the task of improving parliament rests upon the hon. members who are here.
It rests upon us on both sides, in all parties, and I urge that we accept this as a challenge. The people of Canada do not need to pick another 265 people to do this job. If they throw us all out and elect another 265 they will get average Canadians, just as they have got here now. I think we have the stuff in us. I believe we have in us, we who are here, the interest in parliament, both in its greatness in the past and in its possibilities today, to do the job. So this is my plea, that we get the committee set up as quickly as we can, that we call upon it to do a job to improve the rules, but that we, the 265 members who are here, should resolve to exercise a sense of responsibility, and a sense of discipline to try to make this parliament the place it ought to be.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I should like to speak very briefly on this motion to set up a committee, with Mr. Speaker, for

the consideration of the procedure and organization of this house.
I wish to say on behalf of the Social Credit party that even the wording of this resolution speaks well for something which we in this party believe ought to be done, that is, continuing committees from one session to the next within the same parliament.
We can think back to last December. We remember the rush there was in a number of the standing committees to complete their work and make some kind of recommendation to the house before prorogation so that all the work they had done would not be lost. The words of the resolution are, in part; "That a special committee be appointed to continue, with Mr. Speaker-" and so on. That, in itself, is significant. I think there are a number of other committees which should be continuing committees from one session to the next. One that comes to mind first of all is the committee on privileges and elections. We had the task last session of reviewing many aspects of the Canada Elections Act. In addition, there were a number of other matters referred to that committee by the house, and there was definitely a great rush to try to get some kind of recommendation together so that all the work which had been done would not be lost.
When one goes back through the debates over the years he finds, almost every year, a large section of the index to Hansard devoted to procedure. I think this is natural, because with each passing year we find there are changes which are necessary in order to modernize the procedure and organization of this parliament.
We hear a great deal of criticism to the effect that parliament wastes a lot of time. I think there may be some validity to this contention. But I also feel that parliament is the place where questions of policy ought to be discussed; it is a place where there needs to be a great deal of discussion in order that the opinions of those who represent Canadians from one coast to another may be gathered together. Even though one might not agree with some of the things hon. members are saying, or when the subject is unfamiliar to us-for example, representatives from British Columbia or Newfoundland may be speaking on matters which are of little interest to members from other parts of the country-I think we should respect the right of these people. After all, they are representatives of the Canadian electors, and have the right and duty to bring these matters before parliament. I do not at all think it is a waste of time, as has been suggested by some critics.
Along with many other hon. members I deplore repetition and abuse of the rules. I

feel as strongly about this as anyone. But there still remains the right of members to express their opinions here on the floor of the house. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), that perhaps the debate on the resolution stage preceding money bills could be eliminated. I have noticed that there is, at times at least, a great deal of repetition, that the same views are expressed on the resolution stage and then on the first clause of the bill when it comes up before the committee of the whole. Perhaps the resolution stage could be eliminated.
There is another point I should like to bring to the attention of the house. It has to do with want of confidence motions. I think it would constitute a great improvement to the debates in this house if the amendments to supply motions, in particular, but also to the motion for the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and at the end of the budget debate, could mean what they say-in other words, if the effect of passing them would, in fact, bring about the situation envisaged by the literal wording of the amendments. I do not want to be misunderstood. I think it is necessary for a want of confidence motion to be moved at the outset of each session. This is, of course, what is done at the end of the debate on the address. I think an amendment should say what it means. It should express a want of confidence in the government, if that is the intention. As things are, by saying, for example, that the sales tax should be rescinded, we create, through the press, in the minds of people throughout this great country of Canada, the delusion that this is what the debate is about, though in fact every one of the members here knows that if the amendment were supported it would certainly not rescind the sales tax, even though those words form part of the amendment. I think it would be well for us to define more carefully the effect which such motions, or amendments, would have if they were passed.
I also believe that more matters could and should be referred to the standing committees early in the session. We had a very bad experience last year when five or six standing committees that I can think of were meeting, not once or twice but, sometimes, three times a day during the last few days of the session in an attempt to complete their recommendations before parliament prorogued. It was physically impossible for members to attend to the duties they had assumed in these committees and at the same time be present in the house. Some means must be found of bringing about an improvement in this situation, whether it is done by changing the rules or whether it is done through some change of attitude or discipline on the part of the members of the opposition, as well as
Procedure Committee
on the part of government supporters. We know that in the past, whether under Conservative or Liberal administration, there were delays in setting up these committees, delays which brought about the confusion and rush at the end of the session. I think it would constitute a great improvement if the committees were set up as soon as possible so that they could get their work under way. There are a number of standing committees to which references could usefully be made right now.
There has been some discussion about the question period which takes place each day when orders of the day are called. I am one of those who believe that this is one of the most useful periods of the entire day. I think there is some need for greater discipline on the part of members of the opposition in asking questions and, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I think some criticism can properly be directed at hon. members on the treasury benches for skirting around some of these questions and giving incomplete answers-or, in some cases, replies which are not answers at all. I believe in this respect that the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition might be a good one, namely that we might follow the example of Westminster and limit the time during which questions could be asked to, perhaps, 30 minutes. Then, if members were not satisfied with the answers, at the hour of adjournment they could proceed further. I think this could be tried on a trial and approval basis in the first instance, and if it proved satisfactory we would have additional time during the day to proceed with government business.
I agree with most of the things said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) respecting discipline. I think that, no matter how good the rules may be when they are written or rewritten, unless there is discipline and respect for the purpose and function of parliament by members of the opposition and members of the government, particularly of the treasury benches, we will not have any really satisfactory results. I think, too, we could lengthen the hours of sitting. One or two suggestions were made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this regard. Perhaps, also, we could sit in the mornings more often than we do at the present time. With regard to lengthening the number of sitting hours, there should be some means of allowing members to get back more often to the people they represent so they may spend more time in their constituencies and thereby more accurately reflect the opinions of those people who in fact sent them here to express those

Consumer Credit Committee opinions. The Australian parliament has, I think, some good ideas in this respect. I think they sit for three weeks and then adjourn for one week. We would not have to shorten the number of sitting hours; we could lengthen those hours so that perhaps we could sit as many hours in three weeks as we do now in four weeks. I make this suggestion because I think it is extremely important that members from constituencies as far away as mine-and there are some who are still further away, who represent constituencies as far distant as 2,000 to 2,500 miles-should have time to go back and talk to their constituents so they may in fact more accurately represent them in this house.
Mr. Speaker, I just want to add the support of my party to the resolution dealing with the setting up of this committee. I hope the committee will get under way as quickly as possible and will report back to the house with recommendations which will in fact expedite and improve the operation of the house.
